1	# Alioth vs gem5: Architectural Comparison
2	
3	High-level contrast of the two simulators along the dimensions that matter when
4	choosing or extending either one. Focus is on abstractions and design
5	decisions, not class-level or file-level implementation.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 0. At a Glance
10	
11	| Dimension              | Alioth                                              | gem5                                                 |
12	|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
13	| Primary purpose        | Vendor performance-eval lib for Andes RISC-V IPs    | Open multi-ISA architecture research simulator       |
14	| Audience               | IP designers + customers correlating with RTL       | Academia + industry for design-space exploration     |
15	| Sim kernel             | SystemC + custom `afw` tick-tock layer              | Custom discrete-event kernel (event queue)           |
16	| Time model             | Clock-aligned, synchronous cur/nxt commit per tick  | Free-running ticks (ps), event-scheduled             |
17	| ISA semantics          | Out-of-band ISS (vendor `iss-lib` via `iss_adapter`)| In-tree, DSL-generated decoder + execute per ISA     |
18	| CPU model spectrum     | Atomic + per-variant cycle-accurate pipelines       | Atomic, TimingSimple, Minor (in-order), O3, KVM      |
19	| Mid-sim CPU swap       | Not supported                                       | First-class (warmup -> detailed)                     |
20	| Memory system          | Vendor-specific MSS (cache, MSHR, LFB, WB, PL2, HVM)| Classic monolithic XOR Ruby (protocol DSL + NoC)     |
21	| Coherence              | ACE (production, fixed)                             | SLICC-described protocols (user-defined) or classic  |
22	| Module / wiring        | `afw::Module` + `Interface`/`InPort`/`OutPort`/TLM  | `SimObject` + `RequestPort`/`ResponsePort` + Packet  |
23	| Configuration          | YAML + CCI broker, external/internal/customer split | Python config API + auto-generated PyBind11 bindings |
24	| Statistics             | Clarity pipeline DB, HPM (int/ext), spdlog, VCD/FST | Unified Stat framework (scalar/vector/hist/formula)  |
25	| Execution modes        | Bare-metal + semihosting; RTL co-sim                | Syscall Emulation (SE) and Full System (FS)          |
26	| Workload               | ELF per hart                                        | ELF (SE) or kernel + disk image (FS)                 |
27	| Checkpointing          | None                                                | First-class (serialize all SimObject state)          |
28	| Multi-core             | Cluster of variant cores + shared cache (CM500)     | SMP/heterogeneous via Ruby + Garnet NoC topologies   |
29	| NoC                    | Not modeled                                         | Garnet (mesh/torus, virtual channels, routers)       |
30	| Extension model        | Add core variant; pipelines mostly re-implemented   | Out-of-tree SimObjects; SLICC for new protocols      |
31	| Build / langs          | CMake + Conan + C++23 + YAML                        | SCons + C++17 + Python + SLICC + ISA DSL             |
32	| Hot-path discipline    | Codified (`InplaceLog`, `InplaceClarity`, no-heap)  | Per-component; no project-wide discipline            |
33	| RTL co-simulation      | First-class via TLM                                 | Not a core feature                                   |
34	| Distribution           | Vendor-internal (Gitea), customer/internal layering | Open source, public community                        |
35	
36	---
37	
38	## 1. Purpose and Scope
39	
40	**Alioth** is a vendor-built performance evaluation library for Andes IPs
41	(AX46, AX45, AX50, D23V cores plus surrounding fabric). Its north star is
42	*correlate with RTL within a small CPI gap* so customers can size cache
43	hierarchies, vector units, and memory controllers before tapeout. The codebase
44	ships customer-facing and internal-only knobs as separate config layers, and
45	its observability stack (Clarity DB, HPM counters) maps directly to features
46	RTL designers expect to find.
47	
48	**gem5** is a general-purpose computer architecture research simulator. It
49	spans multiple ISAs (RISC-V, ARM, x86, SPARC, MIPS, POWER), multiple
50	abstraction levels in a single binary, and full-system Linux boot. Its design
51	optimizes for *flexibility* and *publishability* - swapping CPU models,
52	writing new coherence protocols in a DSL, comparing topologies. RTL alignment
53	is not a primary use case.
54	
55	This positioning explains nearly every other contrast in this document.
56	
57	---
58	
59	## 2. Simulation Kernel and Time Model
60	
61	| Aspect              | Alioth                                  | gem5                                          |
62	|---------------------|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
63	| Kernel              | SystemC delta-cycle event scheduler      | Custom event queue (`EventQueue`)              |
64	| Time grain          | Bound to clock period (configurable)     | Picoseconds via 64-bit `Tick`                  |
65	| Synchronization     | Global `tick` event + `Tock()` commit    | Per-event scheduling, no global clock          |
66	| Cycle abstraction   | `afw::State<T>` with `.cur` / `.nxt`     | `ClockedObject` + per-object phases            |
67	| Parallelism         | SystemC threads in one OS thread         | Optional parallel mode with `simQuantum`       |
68	
69	Alioth layers a strict **tick-tock** discipline on top of SystemC. A single
70	`Tocker` thread fires on the clock edge, walks every registered `afw::State`,
71	and commits `.nxt` into `.cur` in lockstep. Modules wait on
72	`tick & port_event_list` so that data becomes visible at fixed cycle
73	boundaries. The model behaves like RTL at the cycle level even though the
74	underlying scheduler is event-driven. The cost is that "cur vs nxt" timing
75	must be reasoned about explicitly; the benefit is RTL-like predictability.
76	
77	gem5 takes the opposite stance: there is no global clock that paces all
78	objects, only a global priority queue of events and per-object clock domains.
79	A cache miss schedules a response event at `now + latency`; nothing forces all
80	state to commit at the same instant. This is cheaper to write and faster to
81	run for loose timing, but harder to align with RTL waveforms.
82	
83	---
84	
85	## 3. ISA Model and Instruction Execution
86	
87	This is one of the largest architectural splits between the two simulators.
88	
89	**Alioth** treats ISA semantics as an **out-of-band concern**. Each hart owns
90	an `IssAdapter` that wraps the vendor's functional `iss-lib` (a separately
91	maintained spike-derived ISS). The Alioth pipeline models *only timing*: it
92	schedules fetch, decode, issue, execute, and commit, while the ISS holds
93	architectural state and produces the side effects (register writes, memory
94	ops, exceptions) at commit. Decoder logic, CSR handling, FP/V extensions, and
95	trap behavior live entirely in the ISS, not in the pipeline model. This
96	keeps the timing model lean and lets the same ISS power RTL co-simulation as
97	the golden reference.
98	
99	**gem5** treats ISA semantics as **in-tree, generated code**. An ISA
100	description DSL (`.isa` files: bitfields, decoder, operands) is compiled into
101	C++ decoder state machines and per-instruction execute functions. Each CPU
102	model invokes `StaticInst::execute(ExecContext)`; the same execute function
103	runs under AtomicSimpleCPU, TimingSimpleCPU, MinorCPU, or O3CPU. The
104	*execution context* abstracts away the CPU model. This is the mechanism that
105	lets gem5 swap CPU models mid-simulation: the ISA layer is identical, only
106	the surrounding pipeline machinery changes.
107	
108	Implication: adding a new RISC-V extension is a *config / submodule update*
109	in Alioth (changes flow through iss-lib) but a *codegen + ISA file edit* in
110	gem5. Conversely, prototyping a microarchitecture for a brand-new ISA is
111	natural in gem5 and unnatural in Alioth.
112	
113	---
114	
115	## 4. CPU Model Spectrum
116	
117	Both projects span functional to detailed models, but with different
118	philosophies.
119	
120	### gem5
121	
122	| Model            | Abstraction        | Use                                       |
123	|------------------|--------------------|--------------------------------------------|
124	| AtomicSimpleCPU  | Functional         | Fastest path, fast-forward, OS boot        |
125	| TimingSimpleCPU  | Single-cycle issue, timing memory | Cache-hierarchy studies     |
126	| MinorCPU         | In-order pipeline  | ARM/ embedded perf studies                 |
127	| O3CPU            | Out-of-order superscalar | Detailed perf studies                |
128	| KvmCPU           | Native via KVM     | Boot Linux at near-native speed            |
129	
130	gem5's key idea is that these are **swappable behind one interface**. A
131	typical experiment boots Linux on KVM, warms up caches with AtomicSimpleCPU,
132	then switches to O3CPU for measurement.
133	
134	### Alioth
135	
136	| Model       | Abstraction               | Use                                         |
137	|-------------|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
138	| AtomicCpu   | Functional, zero pipeline | RTL co-sim driver, fast functional sanity   |
139	| AX45 / AX46 / AX50 / D23V | Cycle-accurate per-IP pipelines | Performance evaluation vs RTL |
140	
141	Alioth's models are **product-aligned, not abstraction-aligned**: each
142	cycle-accurate variant corresponds to a real IP. There is no in-order vs
143	out-of-order knob, no "make this one less detailed" mode. Mid-simulation
144	switching is not supported; warmup is done by running through the workload
145	prefix or by relying on the workload's natural warmup.
146	
147	---
148	
149	## 5. Memory Subsystem and Coherence
150	
151	### Alioth: vendor-specific, fixed protocol
152	
153	The AX46 MSS bundles I/D caches, MSHRs, store buffer, eviction buffer,
154	write-near-address buffer, line-fill buffer, optional private L2 with its own
155	MSHR and prefetcher, and a dedicated **HVM** (High-bandwidth Vector Memory)
156	fabric for vector loads/stores. These are *named, hardwired components* with
157	config-driven sizing. Coherence is handled by an **ACE** subsystem (AXI
158	Coherency Extensions) that snoops, tracks line state, and arbitrates
159	write-backs. ACE can be disabled for non-coherent designs. TLM 2.0 AT
160	protocol is used only at MSS boundaries (system memory, devices, external
161	fabric); internal MSS-to-pipeline traffic uses lighter `afw::Interface`
162	method calls.
163	
164	You cannot replace ACE with a different protocol without rewriting the
165	coherence stack. You can configure its parameters.
166	
167	### gem5: two interchangeable memory systems
168	
169	**Classic** memory system: traditional, monolithic. Caches communicate via
170	`Packet` over `RequestPort`/`ResponsePort`. Coherence is implemented inside
171	the cache controller (snoop-based). Fast to set up, less flexible.
172	
173	**Ruby** memory system: protocol-driven. The user writes cache coherence
174	protocols in **SLICC** (Specification Language for Implementing Cache
175	Coherency), a DSL that generates C++ state machines. Stock protocols include
176	MOESI_CMP_directory, MOESI_hammer, MESI_Two_Level, MI_example. The
177	interconnect is modeled by **Garnet**, a configurable NoC with routers,
178	links, and virtual channels - topologies (mesh, torus, custom) are
179	declarative. DRAM timing plugs in via `MemInterface` (built-in models or
180	DRAMsim2/3).
181	
182	Implication: studying *coherence protocols* or *NoC topologies* is gem5's
183	home turf. Studying *one vendor's L1+L2+ACE in cycle-detail* is Alioth's.
184	
185	---
186	
187	## 6. Module / Object Model
188	
189	| Aspect                 | Alioth                                            | gem5                                       |
190	|------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
191	| Root                   | `sc_module` -> `LogModule` -> `afw::Module`        | `SimObject` (-> `ClockedObject`)            |
192	| Wiring primitives      | `Interface` (methods), `InPort`/`OutPort` (events), TLM sockets | `RequestPort` / `ResponsePort` + `Packet`   |
193	| Clocked state          | `afw::State<T>` with explicit `.cur` / `.nxt`     | Free fields; commit timing is per-event     |
194	| Serialization          | Not built in                                       | Every SimObject implements `serialize()`    |
195	| Discovery              | Class-template specialization + variant of cores  | Auto-generated Python params + PyBind11     |
196	
197	Alioth offers **three coupling mechanisms by intent**:
198	
199	- `afw::Interface` (`to_initiator()` / `to_target()`): direct method calls
200	  for tight, per-cycle paths inside a core.
201	- `InPort` / `OutPort`: ready/valid-style signals and event notification.
202	- TLM 2.0 sockets: at IP boundaries (system memory, devices, RTL co-sim).
203	
204	Choosing the right mechanism is a design choice; misuse (e.g., TLM where an
205	Interface would do) shows up as wasted simulation time. The framework
206	enforces the discipline through naming conventions and design rules.
207	
208	gem5 unifies almost everything around **ports + packets**. A `Packet`
209	carries a request through phases (`recvTimingReq`, `recvTimingResp`,
210	`recvFunctional`, `recvAtomic`); the same port plugs into a cache, a bus, a
211	crossbar, or a memory. This is more uniform but loses the per-cycle
212	fast-path that Alioth's Interface mechanism provides.
213	
214	---
215	
216	## 7. Configuration System
217	
218	| Aspect       | Alioth                                                | gem5                                          |
219	|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
220	| Surface      | YAML files (`.cfg.yml`) + CLI overrides                | Python script that instantiates SimObjects    |
221	| Backend      | CCI broker; `afw::ParamTyped<T>`, `afw::CustomerParamTyped<T>` | Auto-generated `Params` struct + PyBind11 |
222	| Layering     | External (customer) + internal (vendor) + per-cluster | Pure Python composition; user-defined layers   |
223	| Validation   | Per-param spec with ranges/enums/units                | Python-level + per-SimObject ctor checks       |
224	| Reproducibility | YAML + CLI archived; `--cluster-type` selects backend | Python script + `--debug-flags` archived       |
225	
226	The contrast is fundamentally **data vs code**:
227	
228	- Alioth's YAML config is *static* and *audit-friendly*. A customer can read
229	  it and a tool can validate it without executing Python. The external /
230	  internal split is enforced by the `WhiteBoxCluster` / `AndesCluster` /
231	  `VerificationCluster` triplet so customer visibility is part of the API.
232	- gem5's Python config is *programmable*. A script can sweep a parameter
233	  with a for-loop, build heterogeneous systems, or branch on environment
234	  variables. The cost is that "what was actually simulated" requires reading
235	  a script, not just a flat file.
236	
237	---
238	
239	## 8. Statistics and Observability
240	
241	Both simulators emit cycle counts, miss rates, and per-component counters,
242	but the output models differ.
243	
244	**Alioth** has three coordinated channels:
245	
246	1. **Clarity DB**: a pipeline-level event database. Per-cycle, per-stage,
247	   per-instruction state can be dumped, with start/stop conditions to scope
248	   the recording window. This is the workhorse for cycle-by-cycle alignment
249	   with RTL FSDB waveforms.
250	2. **HPM counters**: internal HPM (microarchitectural - stall reasons, MSHR
251	   occupancy, FIFO depths) and external HPM (customer-visible counters
252	   matching the IP's documented PMC set). Sampled at configurable intervals.
253	3. **spdlog structured logs**: `[Tag] evt=<ns>.<action> key=value` records
254	   with allow-list filtering by module instance.
255	
256	Plus optional **waveform output** (VCD/FST) for SystemC signals.
257	
258	**gem5** has a **unified `Stats` framework**: every SimObject registers
259	scalars, vectors (per-thread/CPU), histograms, distributions, or formulas
260	(derived). At end-of-simulation (or on `dumpStats()`), everything is written
261	to a single text or CSV file. Probes give event-driven hooks. There is no
262	direct equivalent of Clarity's pipeline DB; cycle-level detail in gem5
263	typically comes from O3 trace flags + post-processing.
264	
265	The asymmetry reflects the priorities: gem5 optimizes for *comparison across
266	runs* (one number per stat), Alioth for *waveform-level forensics on one
267	run*.
268	
269	---
270	
271	## 9. Execution Modes and Workload
272	
273	| Mode            | Alioth                          | gem5                                    |
274	|-----------------|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
275	| Bare-metal      | Yes (semihosting via ebreak)    | Yes                                      |
276	| Syscall emulation | No                              | Yes (SE mode)                            |
277	| Full-system OS  | No                              | Yes (FS mode, boots Linux + disk image) |
278	| RTL co-sim      | First-class via TLM             | Not a primary feature                    |
279	| Checkpointing   | No                              | Yes (full state, swap CPU on restore)    |
280	
281	Alioth's workload model is **one or more ELFs**, one per hart, loaded into
282	simulated memory; semihosting traps handle exit/print/file I/O. There is no
283	file system, no kernel, no syscall emulation. This matches the IP-validation
284	use case: run a kernel of code, measure cycles, compare with RTL.
285	
286	gem5 spans both **SE** (single ELF, syscalls emulated by the simulator) and
287	**FS** (real OS boot with modeled devices: UART, timer, disk, NIC). FS mode
288	is what makes "boot Linux, measure SPECint" possible. Checkpointing
289	underpins the practical workflow: fast-forward functionally, take a
290	checkpoint at the region of interest, then restore on a detailed CPU.
291	
292	---
293	
294	## 10. Multi-Core, Cluster, Interconnect
295	
296	**Alioth** organizes multiple cores into an `InternalCluster` whose `cores`
297	field is a `std::variant` of every supported CPU type. Heterogeneous mixes
298	(some AX46, some D23v) are allowed. Cores share a system-memory initiator
299	socket and optionally a coherent shared cache (e.g., CM500). Coherence is
300	maintained by snooping plus the shared cache controller. There is **no
301	parameterized NoC**: cores talk through fixed fabrics with configurable
302	parameters, not user-described topologies. The three cluster variants
303	(`WhiteBox`, `Andes`, `Verification`) differ in *config visibility*, not in
304	*topology*.
305	
306	**gem5** treats SMP as N CPU SimObjects sharing a memory system. With Ruby +
307	Garnet, the user describes the on-chip network as a topology object - a
308	mesh, torus, point-to-point, or custom routing - with router and link
309	parameters. Coherence and interconnect are independent dimensions of the
310	design space. This is gem5's strongest differentiator for NoC and CMP
311	research.
312	
313	---
314	
315	## 11. Extension Model
316	
317	**Adding a new core variant to Alioth**: create
318	`src/model/<variant>/...` modules, derive from `BaseCpuTopTemplate<DynInst>`,
319	register in the cluster variant, write config specs. The framework
320	(`afw::State`, `afw::Interface`, ports, TLM adapters) is reusable; pipeline
321	stages, LSU, ROB tend to be **re-implemented per variant** because
322	microarchitectures differ enough that abstraction would lose detail. IFU and
323	MSS components are often shared across closely related variants.
324	
325	**Adding a new component to gem5**: subclass `SimObject` (or `BaseCPU`,
326	`BaseCache`, `Device`), implement port callbacks, declare the params; the
327	build system auto-generates Python bindings. New coherence protocols are
328	*SLICC files* under `src/mem/ruby/protocol/`. Out-of-tree development is
329	explicitly supported. The cost of this flexibility is that gem5 is a
330	larger surface to learn, and protocols/CPU models have visible inheritance
331	contracts you must satisfy.
332	
333	---
334	
335	## 12. Build, Dependencies, Languages
336	
337	| Aspect           | Alioth                                            | gem5                                     |
338	|------------------|----------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
339	| Build system     | CMake (Ninja/Make) + `lazy_build.sh` wrapper       | SCons                                     |
340	| Dependency mgmt  | Conan (SystemC 2.3.3 / 2.3.4 / 3.0.2 selectable)   | Bundled + system packages                 |
341	| Core language    | C++23 (gnu23 default, gnu17 fallback)              | C++17                                     |
342	| Other languages  | YAML (config)                                      | Python (config), SLICC (protocols), ISA DSL |
343	| Code generation  | None (all hand-written)                            | ISA DSL -> decoder/execute; SLICC -> C++  |
344	| Sanitizers       | ASan, UBSan, LSan, TSan via build levels           | Available, less centralized               |
345	
346	Alioth's build story focuses on **reproducibility and SystemC version
347	mobility**: Conan pins SystemC versions; multiple build sets (release,
348	debug, regression, perf) toggle assertions, logging, and profiling flags
349	deterministically. gem5's build relies on SCons to coordinate ISA codegen
350	and SLICC compilation, which is the price of its DSL-driven flexibility.
351	
352	---
353	
354	## 13. Performance Discipline
355	
356	This is a subtle but important contrast. Both simulators run lots of cycles;
357	how they treat per-cycle cost differs.
358	
359	**Alioth codifies hot-path discipline as project rules**:
360	
361	- `InplaceLog<level>(lambda)` defers arg evaluation when logging is off.
362	- `InplaceClarity(lambda)` does the same for pipeline DB recording.
363	- "No heap allocation in hot paths" is a review rule, not a suggestion.
364	- Containers prefer contiguous storage; `std::map`/`std::set` are flagged.
365	- `std::function` allocation is documented as a known overhead.
366	- A dedicated `coding-simulator.md` rule file accumulates each new
367	  micro-pattern as it is found.
368	
369	This discipline pays for itself when you must match RTL on long traces
370	(billions of cycles) without sub-linear scaling.
371	
372	**gem5** has no project-wide equivalent. Individual components have been
373	tuned over the years, but heap allocations in event handlers, free use of
374	STL maps, and unguarded debug formatting are common. gem5 is fast enough
375	for most academic workloads (especially with checkpointing skipping long
376	warmup), so the cost of looser discipline is bounded by the typical
377	workload length.
378	
379	---
380	
381	## 14. Where Each One Shines
382	
383	**Choose Alioth when**:
384	
385	- You need cycle-level alignment with RTL of a specific Andes IP.
386	- You want a customer/internal config split with audit-friendly YAML.
387	- Your workloads are bare-metal kernels, not Linux applications.
388	- You care about long-trace performance discipline.
389	- You need pipeline-level forensics (Clarity DB) alongside HPM counters.
390	
391	**Choose gem5 when**:
392	
393	- You are exploring a design space across ISAs, CPU models, coherence
394	  protocols, or interconnect topologies.
395	- You need full-system Linux boot or syscall emulation.
396	- You want to write a new coherence protocol declaratively (SLICC).
397	- You need checkpointing and mid-simulation CPU swaps for tractable runs.
398	- You publish or share results in an open community.
399	
400	The two are largely **non-overlapping**: Alioth is a production correlation
401	tool for one vendor's IPs; gem5 is a research/exploration platform across
402	ISAs and protocols.
403	
404	---
405	
406	## 15. Key Takeaways
407	
408	1. **Time discipline**: Alioth enforces a tick-tock cycle on top of
409	   SystemC's event scheduler; gem5 is pure event-driven with per-object
410	   clocks.
411	2. **ISA placement**: Alioth keeps ISA semantics out-of-band (vendor ISS);
412	   gem5 generates ISA + decoder + execute from a DSL inside the simulator.
413	3. **Memory + coherence**: Alioth ships one production memory subsystem
414	   with ACE coherence; gem5 ships a research-grade alternative (SLICC +
415	   Garnet) where protocol and topology are user-described.
416	4. **Configuration**: Alioth uses static YAML with a customer/internal
417	   visibility split; gem5 uses programmable Python composition.
418	5. **Modes**: Alioth runs bare-metal ELFs with first-class RTL co-sim;
419	   gem5 runs SE or full-system Linux with checkpointing.
420	6. **Extension**: Alioth re-implements pipelines per variant; gem5 makes
421	   out-of-tree SimObjects and SLICC protocols cheap.
422	7. **Performance discipline**: Alioth codifies per-cycle hot-path rules in
423	   the project; gem5 does not.
424	
425	Same family of "cycle-level architectural simulators", different optimization
426	targets.
427

# Alioth vs gem5: Architectural Comparison

High-level contrast of the two simulators along the dimensions that matter when
choosing or extending either one. Focus is on abstractions and design
decisions, not class-level or file-level implementation.

---

## 0. At a Glance

| Dimension              | Alioth                                              | gem5                                                 |
|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| Primary purpose        | Vendor performance-eval lib for Andes RISC-V IPs    | Open multi-ISA architecture research simulator       |
| Audience               | IP designers + customers correlating with RTL       | Academia + industry for design-space exploration     |
| Sim kernel             | SystemC + custom `afw` tick-tock layer              | Custom discrete-event kernel (event queue)           |
| Time model             | Clock-aligned, synchronous cur/nxt commit per tick  | Free-running ticks (ps), event-scheduled             |
| ISA semantics          | Out-of-band ISS (vendor `iss-lib` via `iss_adapter`)| In-tree, DSL-generated decoder + execute per ISA     |
| CPU model spectrum     | Atomic + per-variant cycle-accurate pipelines       | Atomic, TimingSimple, Minor (in-order), O3, KVM      |
| Mid-sim CPU swap       | Not supported                                       | First-class (warmup -> detailed)                     |
| Memory system          | Vendor-specific MSS (cache, MSHR, LFB, WB, PL2, HVM)| Classic monolithic XOR Ruby (protocol DSL + NoC)     |
| Coherence              | ACE (production, fixed)                             | SLICC-described protocols (user-defined) or classic  |
| Module / wiring        | `afw::Module` + `Interface`/`InPort`/`OutPort`/TLM  | `SimObject` + `RequestPort`/`ResponsePort` + Packet  |
| Configuration          | YAML + CCI broker, external/internal/customer split | Python config API + auto-generated PyBind11 bindings |
| Statistics             | Clarity pipeline DB, HPM (int/ext), spdlog, VCD/FST | Unified Stat framework (scalar/vector/hist/formula)  |
| Execution modes        | Bare-metal + semihosting; RTL co-sim                | Syscall Emulation (SE) and Full System (FS)          |
| Workload               | ELF per hart                                        | ELF (SE) or kernel + disk image (FS)                 |
| Checkpointing          | None                                                | First-class (serialize all SimObject state)          |
| Multi-core             | Cluster of variant cores + shared cache (CM500)     | SMP/heterogeneous via Ruby + Garnet NoC topologies   |
| NoC                    | Not modeled                                         | Garnet (mesh/torus, virtual channels, routers)       |
| Extension model        | Add core variant; pipelines mostly re-implemented   | Out-of-tree SimObjects; SLICC for new protocols      |
| Build / langs          | CMake + Conan + C++23 + YAML                        | SCons + C++17 + Python + SLICC + ISA DSL             |
| Hot-path discipline    | Codified (`InplaceLog`, `InplaceClarity`, no-heap)  | Per-component; no project-wide discipline            |
| RTL co-simulation      | First-class via TLM                                 | Not a core feature                                   |
| Distribution           | Vendor-internal (Gitea), customer/internal layering | Open source, public community                        |

---

## 1. Purpose and Scope

**Alioth** is a vendor-built performance evaluation library for Andes IPs
(AX46, AX45, AX50, D23V cores plus surrounding fabric). Its north star is
*correlate with RTL within a small CPI gap* so customers can size cache
hierarchies, vector units, and memory controllers before tapeout. The codebase
ships customer-facing and internal-only knobs as separate config layers, and
its observability stack (Clarity DB, HPM counters) maps directly to features
RTL designers expect to find.

**gem5** is a general-purpose computer architecture research simulator. It
spans multiple ISAs (RISC-V, ARM, x86, SPARC, MIPS, POWER), multiple
abstraction levels in a single binary, and full-system Linux boot. Its design
optimizes for *flexibility* and *publishability* - swapping CPU models,
writing new coherence protocols in a DSL, comparing topologies. RTL alignment
is not a primary use case.

This positioning explains nearly every other contrast in this document.

---

## 2. Simulation Kernel and Time Model

| Aspect              | Alioth                                  | gem5                                          |
|---------------------|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Kernel              | SystemC delta-cycle event scheduler      | Custom event queue (`EventQueue`)              |
| Time grain          | Bound to clock period (configurable)     | Picoseconds via 64-bit `Tick`                  |
| Synchronization     | Global `tick` event + `Tock()` commit    | Per-event scheduling, no global clock          |
| Cycle abstraction   | `afw::State<T>` with `.cur` / `.nxt`     | `ClockedObject` + per-object phases            |
| Parallelism         | SystemC threads in one OS thread         | Optional parallel mode with `simQuantum`       |

Alioth layers a strict **tick-tock** discipline on top of SystemC. A single
`Tocker` thread fires on the clock edge, walks every registered `afw::State`,
and commits `.nxt` into `.cur` in lockstep. Modules wait on
`tick & port_event_list` so that data becomes visible at fixed cycle
boundaries. The model behaves like RTL at the cycle level even though the
underlying scheduler is event-driven. The cost is that "cur vs nxt" timing
must be reasoned about explicitly; the benefit is RTL-like predictability.

gem5 takes the opposite stance: there is no global clock that paces all
objects, only a global priority queue of events and per-object clock domains.
A cache miss schedules a response event at `now + latency`; nothing forces all
state to commit at the same instant. This is cheaper to write and faster to
run for loose timing, but harder to align with RTL waveforms.

---

## 3. ISA Model and Instruction Execution

This is one of the largest architectural splits between the two simulators.

**Alioth** treats ISA semantics as an **out-of-band concern**. Each hart owns
an `IssAdapter` that wraps the vendor's functional `iss-lib` (a separately
maintained spike-derived ISS). The Alioth pipeline models *only timing*: it
schedules fetch, decode, issue, execute, and commit, while the ISS holds
architectural state and produces the side effects (register writes, memory
ops, exceptions) at commit. Decoder logic, CSR handling, FP/V extensions, and
trap behavior live entirely in the ISS, not in the pipeline model. This
keeps the timing model lean and lets the same ISS power RTL co-simulation as
the golden reference.

**gem5** treats ISA semantics as **in-tree, generated code**. An ISA
description DSL (`.isa` files: bitfields, decoder, operands) is compiled into
C++ decoder state machines and per-instruction execute functions. Each CPU
model invokes `StaticInst::execute(ExecContext)`; the same execute function
runs under AtomicSimpleCPU, TimingSimpleCPU, MinorCPU, or O3CPU. The
*execution context* abstracts away the CPU model. This is the mechanism that
lets gem5 swap CPU models mid-simulation: the ISA layer is identical, only
the surrounding pipeline machinery changes.

Implication: adding a new RISC-V extension is a *config / submodule update*
in Alioth (changes flow through iss-lib) but a *codegen + ISA file edit* in
gem5. Conversely, prototyping a microarchitecture for a brand-new ISA is
natural in gem5 and unnatural in Alioth.

---

## 4. CPU Model Spectrum

Both projects span functional to detailed models, but with different
philosophies.

### gem5

| Model            | Abstraction        | Use                                       |
|------------------|--------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| AtomicSimpleCPU  | Functional         | Fastest path, fast-forward, OS boot        |
| TimingSimpleCPU  | Single-cycle issue, timing memory | Cache-hierarchy studies     |
| MinorCPU         | In-order pipeline  | ARM/ embedded perf studies                 |
| O3CPU            | Out-of-order superscalar | Detailed perf studies                |
| KvmCPU           | Native via KVM     | Boot Linux at near-native speed            |

gem5's key idea is that these are **swappable behind one interface**. A
typical experiment boots Linux on KVM, warms up caches with AtomicSimpleCPU,
then switches to O3CPU for measurement.

### Alioth

| Model       | Abstraction               | Use                                         |
|-------------|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| AtomicCpu   | Functional, zero pipeline | RTL co-sim driver, fast functional sanity   |
| AX45 / AX46 / AX50 / D23V | Cycle-accurate per-IP pipelines | Performance evaluation vs RTL |

Alioth's models are **product-aligned, not abstraction-aligned**: each
cycle-accurate variant corresponds to a real IP. There is no in-order vs
out-of-order knob, no "make this one less detailed" mode. Mid-simulation
switching is not supported; warmup is done by running through the workload
prefix or by relying on the workload's natural warmup.

---

## 5. Memory Subsystem and Coherence

### Alioth: vendor-specific, fixed protocol

The AX46 MSS bundles I/D caches, MSHRs, store buffer, eviction buffer,
write-near-address buffer, line-fill buffer, optional private L2 with its own
MSHR and prefetcher, and a dedicated **HVM** (High-bandwidth Vector Memory)
fabric for vector loads/stores. These are *named, hardwired components* with
config-driven sizing. Coherence is handled by an **ACE** subsystem (AXI
Coherency Extensions) that snoops, tracks line state, and arbitrates
write-backs. ACE can be disabled for non-coherent designs. TLM 2.0 AT
protocol is used only at MSS boundaries (system memory, devices, external
fabric); internal MSS-to-pipeline traffic uses lighter `afw::Interface`
method calls.

You cannot replace ACE with a different protocol without rewriting the
coherence stack. You can configure its parameters.

### gem5: two interchangeable memory systems

**Classic** memory system: traditional, monolithic. Caches communicate via
`Packet` over `RequestPort`/`ResponsePort`. Coherence is implemented inside
the cache controller (snoop-based). Fast to set up, less flexible.

**Ruby** memory system: protocol-driven. The user writes cache coherence
protocols in **SLICC** (Specification Language for Implementing Cache
Coherency), a DSL that generates C++ state machines. Stock protocols include
MOESI_CMP_directory, MOESI_hammer, MESI_Two_Level, MI_example. The
interconnect is modeled by **Garnet**, a configurable NoC with routers,
links, and virtual channels - topologies (mesh, torus, custom) are
declarative. DRAM timing plugs in via `MemInterface` (built-in models or
DRAMsim2/3).

Implication: studying *coherence protocols* or *NoC topologies* is gem5's
home turf. Studying *one vendor's L1+L2+ACE in cycle-detail* is Alioth's.

---

## 6. Module / Object Model

| Aspect                 | Alioth                                            | gem5                                       |
|------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Root                   | `sc_module` -> `LogModule` -> `afw::Module`        | `SimObject` (-> `ClockedObject`)            |
| Wiring primitives      | `Interface` (methods), `InPort`/`OutPort` (events), TLM sockets | `RequestPort` / `ResponsePort` + `Packet`   |
| Clocked state          | `afw::State<T>` with explicit `.cur` / `.nxt`     | Free fields; commit timing is per-event     |
| Serialization          | Not built in                                       | Every SimObject implements `serialize()`    |
| Discovery              | Class-template specialization + variant of cores  | Auto-generated Python params + PyBind11     |

Alioth offers **three coupling mechanisms by intent**:

- `afw::Interface` (`to_initiator()` / `to_target()`): direct method calls
  for tight, per-cycle paths inside a core.
- `InPort` / `OutPort`: ready/valid-style signals and event notification.
- TLM 2.0 sockets: at IP boundaries (system memory, devices, RTL co-sim).

Choosing the right mechanism is a design choice; misuse (e.g., TLM where an
Interface would do) shows up as wasted simulation time. The framework
enforces the discipline through naming conventions and design rules.

gem5 unifies almost everything around **ports + packets**. A `Packet`
carries a request through phases (`recvTimingReq`, `recvTimingResp`,
`recvFunctional`, `recvAtomic`); the same port plugs into a cache, a bus, a
crossbar, or a memory. This is more uniform but loses the per-cycle
fast-path that Alioth's Interface mechanism provides.

---

## 7. Configuration System

| Aspect       | Alioth                                                | gem5                                          |
|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Surface      | YAML files (`.cfg.yml`) + CLI overrides                | Python script that instantiates SimObjects    |
| Backend      | CCI broker; `afw::ParamTyped<T>`, `afw::CustomerParamTyped<T>` | Auto-generated `Params` struct + PyBind11 |
| Layering     | External (customer) + internal (vendor) + per-cluster | Pure Python composition; user-defined layers   |
| Validation   | Per-param spec with ranges/enums/units                | Python-level + per-SimObject ctor checks       |
| Reproducibility | YAML + CLI archived; `--cluster-type` selects backend | Python script + `--debug-flags` archived       |

The contrast is fundamentally **data vs code**:

- Alioth's YAML config is *static* and *audit-friendly*. A customer can read
  it and a tool can validate it without executing Python. The external /
  internal split is enforced by the `WhiteBoxCluster` / `AndesCluster` /
  `VerificationCluster` triplet so customer visibility is part of the API.
- gem5's Python config is *programmable*. A script can sweep a parameter
  with a for-loop, build heterogeneous systems, or branch on environment
  variables. The cost is that "what was actually simulated" requires reading
  a script, not just a flat file.

---

## 8. Statistics and Observability

Both simulators emit cycle counts, miss rates, and per-component counters,
but the output models differ.

**Alioth** has three coordinated channels:

1. **Clarity DB**: a pipeline-level event database. Per-cycle, per-stage,
   per-instruction state can be dumped, with start/stop conditions to scope

   with RTL FSDB waveforms.
2. **HPM counters**: internal HPM (microarchitectural - stall reasons, MSHR
   occupancy, FIFO depths) and external HPM (customer-visible counters
   matching the IP's documented PMC set). Sampled at configurable intervals.
3. **spdlog structured logs**: `[Tag] evt=<ns>.<action> key=value` records
   with allow-list filtering by module instance.

Plus optional **waveform output** (VCD/FST) for SystemC signals.

The asymmetry reflects the priorities: gem5 optimizes for *comparison across
runs* (one number per stat), Alioth for *waveform-level forensics on one
run*.

---

| Mode            | Alioth                          | gem5                                    |
|-----------------|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Bare-metal      | Yes (semihosting via ebreak)    | Yes                                      |
| Syscall emulation | No                              | Yes (SE mode)                            |
| Full-system OS  | No                              | Yes (FS mode, boots Linux + disk image) |
| RTL co-sim      | First-class via TLM             | Not a primary feature                    |
| Checkpointing   | No                              | Yes (full state, swap CPU on restore)    |

---

design space. This is gem5's strongest differentiator for NoC and CMP
research.

---

## 11. Extension Model

**Adding a new core variant to Alioth**: create
`src/model/<variant>/...` modules, derive from `BaseCpuTopTemplate<DynInst>`,
register in the cluster variant, write config specs. The framework
(`afw::State`, `afw::Interface`, ports, TLM adapters) is reusable; pipeline

explicitly supported. The cost of this flexibility is that gem5 is a
larger surface to learn, and protocols/CPU models have visible inheritance
contracts you must satisfy.

---

## 12. Build, Dependencies, Languages

| Aspect           | Alioth                                            | gem5                                     |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Build system     | CMake (Ninja/Make) + `lazy_build.sh` wrapper       | SCons                                     |
| Dependency mgmt  | Conan (SystemC 2.3.3 / 2.3.4 / 3.0.2 selectable)   | Bundled + system packages                 |
| Core language    | C++23 (gnu23 default, gnu17 fallback)              | C++17                                     |
| Other languages  | YAML (config)                                      | Python (config), SLICC (protocols), ISA DSL |
| Code generation  | None (all hand-written)                            | ISA DSL -> decoder/execute; SLICC -> C++  |
| Sanitizers       | ASan, UBSan, LSan, TSan via build levels           | Available, less centralized               |

Alioth's build story focuses on **reproducibility and SystemC version
mobility**: Conan pins SystemC versions; multiple build sets (release,
debug, regression, perf) toggle assertions, logging, and profiling flags
deterministically. gem5's build relies on SCons to coordinate ISA codegen
and SLICC compilation, which is the price of its DSL-driven flexibility.

---

## 13. Performance Discipline

This is a subtle but important contrast. Both simulators run lots of cycles;
how they treat per-cycle cost differs.

**Alioth codifies hot-path discipline as project rules**:

- `InplaceLog<level>(lambda)` defers arg evaluation when logging is off.
- `InplaceClarity(lambda)` does the same for pipeline DB recording.
- "No heap allocation in hot paths" is a review rule, not a suggestion.
- Containers prefer contiguous storage; `std::map`/`std::set` are flagged.
- `std::function` allocation is documented as a known overhead.
- A dedicated `coding-simulator.md` rule file accumulates each new
  micro-pattern as it is found.

This discipline pays for itself when you must match RTL on long traces
(billions of cycles) without sub-linear scaling.

**gem5** has no project-wide equivalent. Individual components have been
tuned over the years, but heap allocations in event handlers, free use of
STL maps, and unguarded debug formatting are common. gem5 is fast enough
for most academic workloads (especially with checkpointing skipping long
warmup), so the cost of looser discipline is bounded by the typical
workload length.

---

## 14. Where Each One Shines

**Choose Alioth when**:

- You need cycle-level alignment with RTL of a specific Andes IP.
- You want a customer/internal config split with audit-friendly YAML.
- Your workloads are bare-metal kernels, not Linux applications.
- You care about long-trace performance discipline.
- You need pipeline-level forensics (Clarity DB) alongside HPM counters.

**Choose gem5 when**:

- You are exploring a design space across ISAs, CPU models, coherence
  protocols, or interconnect topologies.
- You need full-system Linux boot or syscall emulation.
- You want to write a new coherence protocol declaratively (SLICC).
- You need checkpointing and mid-simulation CPU swaps for tractable runs.
- You publish or share results in an open community.

The two are largely **non-overlapping**: Alioth is a production correlation
tool for one vendor's IPs; gem5 is a research/exploration platform across
ISAs and protocols.

---

## 15. Key Takeaways

1. **Time discipline**: Alioth enforces a tick-tock cycle on top of
   SystemC's event scheduler; gem5 is pure event-driven with per-object
   clocks.
2. **ISA placement**: Alioth keeps ISA semantics out-of-band (vendor ISS);
   gem5 generates ISA + decoder + execute from a DSL inside the simulator.
3. **Memory + coherence**: Alioth ships one production memory subsystem
   with ACE coherence; gem5 ships a research-grade alternative (SLICC +
   Garnet) where protocol and topology are user-described.
4. **Configuration**: Alioth uses static YAML with a customer/internal
   visibility split; gem5 uses programmable Python composition.
5. **Modes**: Alioth runs bare-metal ELFs with first-class RTL co-sim;
   gem5 runs SE or full-system Linux with checkpointing.
6. **Extension**: Alioth re-implements pipelines per variant; gem5 makes
   out-of-tree SimObjects and SLICC protocols cheap.
7. **Performance discipline**: Alioth codifies per-cycle hot-path rules in
   the project; gem5 does not.

Same family of "cycle-level architectural simulators", different optimization
targets.

Target-based commands and visibility specifiers 214 - Imported targets for all dependencies 215 - Source file management with helper scripts 216 - C++ standard configuration 217 - Compile definitions and include directories 218 - Library linking patterns 219 - Special cases and practical examples 220 221 ### Maintenance Scripts 222 223 Use `scripts/generate_cmake_sources.sh` to regenerate source file lists after adding or removing source files: 224 225 ```bash 226 # Regenerate cmake/sources.cmake with categorized source variables 227 ./scripts/generate_cmake_sources.sh 228 ``` 229 230 This script scans the `src/` directory and generates `cmake/sources.cmake`, which defines shared source variables used by all build targets: 231 232 - `ALIOTH_CLUSTER_SOURCES` - Cluster module sources 233 - `ALIOTH_CONFIG_SOURCES` - Configuration sources 234 - `ALIOTH_MODEL_SOURCES` - Core model sources (ax46, atomic, d23v, etc.) 235 - `ALIOTH_PLATFORM_IP_SHARED_SOURCES` - Platform IP sources shared by library targets 236 - `ALIOTH_TESTBENCH_SOURCES` - Testbench sources (build_dev only) 237 - `ALIOTH_PLATFORM_IP_INTERNAL_FULL_SOURCES` - Full internal_use sources 238 239 Then copy the generated content into the corresponding `target_sources()` block in CMakeLists.txt. 240 241 ## Directory Structure 242 243 ``` 244 Alioth/ 245 ├── cfg/ # Configuration parameters for modules 246 ├── lib/ # Framework-related files 247 └── src/ 248 ├── main.cpp # Main entry point with top model selection 249 ├── cli.cpp # Configuration and parameter parsing 250 ├── model/ 251 │ ├── interface/ # Interfaces between modules 252 │ ├── tool/ # Common utility functions 253 │ ├── top/ # Different top model combinations 254 │ └── vip/ # Virtual IPs for validation 255 └── sim/ # Simulator components and adapters 256 ``` 257 258 ## Commit Guidelines 259 260 ### Format 261 ``` 262 type[scope]: description 263 264 [optional body] 265 266 [optional footer] 267 ``` 268 269 ### Types 270 - **build**: Changes affecting build system or dependencies 271 - **chore**: Updates to tasks with no production code change 272 - **ci**: Changes to CI configuration 273 - **docs**: Documentation changes 274 - **feat**: New feature (PATCH in semantic versioning) 275 - **fix**: Bug fix (MINOR in semantic versioning) 276 - **modify**: Adjustments to existing features 277 - **perf**: Performance improvements 278 - **refactor**: Code changes that neither fix bugs nor add features 279 - **style**: Changes not affecting code meaning 280 - **test**: Adding or correcting tests 281 - **revert**: Reverting previous commits 282 283 ### Scopes 284 Indicate modules being modified: frontend, core, mss, vpu, ace, adapter, framework, misc, pl 285 286 ### Examples 287 ``` 288 feat[framework]: update top for multi-top and add AX47Cpu for Event-driven module 289 290 feat[vpu]: implement vdis module and refine some vru module 291 ``` 292 293 > This section only describes the **Git commit message format**. 294 > For coding rule and standards, please 295 > - Refer to **[doc/cfg-file-format.md](doc/cfg-file-format.md)** to edit config files under `./cfg` 296 > - Refer to **[Performance model coding rules (OneNote)](https://andesone.sharepoint.com/sites/Alioth/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7Bcebbeef8-135f-4f41-9dac-665c9eb2ecc4%7D&action=edit&wd=target%28Framework.one%7Cbb8739db-e563-499c-950d-740f0ac45599%2FPerf+model+coding+rules%7C1fc67f2a-1032-4689-b071-a318baeaac3b%2F%29&wdorigin=703)** to develop model 297 298 299 ## Logger Levels 300 301 - **Trace**: Detailed debug information of algorithms/implementations 302 - **Debug**: Detailed debug information of each unit 303 - **Info**: Debug information shared with the team 304 - **Warn**: Unexpected or ambiguous behavior (discuss with unit lead) 305 - **Error**: Invalid input/operation leading to program termination 306 307 ## License Setup 308 When using `--cluster-type andes`, `debug`, or `verification`, remember to export the license file: 309 ```bash 310 # Make sure the current directory is the root of Alioth 311 export ANDESYSC_LICENSE_FILE=$(pwd)/license/node-locked-general.lic 312 ``` 313

`=4`: *-fsanitize=leak -fno-omit-frame-pointer*
`=5`: *-fsanitize=address -fsanitize=leak -fsanitize=undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer* | | **Build Sets** | `-DBUILD_SET=release` | `-Denable_clarity=on -Denable_andesclarity_display_scope=1 -DCOSIM_EN=1 -Denable_log=on -Denable_log_level=3 -Denable_external_hpm=on` | | | `-DBUILD_SET=debug` | `-Denable_clarity=on -Denable_andesclarity_display_scope=2 -DCOSIM_EN=1 -Denable_log=on -Denable_log_level=1 -Denable_external_hpm=on -Denable_internal_hpm=on -Denable_wave=on -Denable_optionalparam=on` | | **Build Flow Types** | `-DBUILD_FLOW_TYPE=build_dev` | Development build (cluster and platform tests) | | | `-DBUILD_FLOW_TYPE=build_dev_lib` | Library-only build | | | `-DBUILD_FLOW_TYPE=build_platform` | Platform-only build (requires library from build_dev_lib) | ### Example Conan for Sanitizer ```bash # Remember to conan with build_type asan (to be updated) ``` ### Example Conan for Debugging ```bash # Remember to conan with build_type debug bash scripts/conan/build.sh debug \ --arch x86 --systemc_version 3.0.2 --os linux \ --compiler clang20 --libc libstdcxx11 \ --cstandard gnu23 --conanfile-variant fmt12-nostdfmt \ --install-prefix conan_install export CONAN_TOOLCHAIN_PATH="$PWD/conan_install/debug/3.0.2/x86/linux/clang/libstdcxx11/gnu23/fmt12-nostdfmt/conan_toolchain.cmake" mkdir -p build_debug && cd build_debug || exit 1 cmake .. -G "Ninja" \ -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE="${CONAN_TOOLCHAIN_PATH}" \ -DCMAKE_POLICY_DEFAULT_CMP0091=NEW \ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \ -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-20 -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++-20 \ -DBUILD_SET=debug cmake --build . --parallel 16 ``` ## This provides better maintainability, clearer dependencies, and improved IDE support. ### Key Principles 1. **Target-based, not global**: Use `target_*` commands instead of global `add_definitions()`, `include_directories()`, etc. 2. **Explicit visibility**: Always specify `PRIVATE`, `PUBLIC`, or `INTERFACE` for target properties 3. **Imported targets**: Use modern imported targets like `Boost::boost`, `SystemC::systemc`, `BZip2::BZip2` 4. **Explicit source lists**: Use `target_sources()` with explicit file lists instead of `file(GLOB_RECURSE)` ### Quick Examples ```cmake # ✅ Modern way add_executable(my_exe) target_sources(my_exe PRIVATE main.cpp utils.cpp) target_compile_features(my_exe PRIVATE cxx_std_17) target_include_directories(my_exe PRIVATE include) target_link_libraries(my_exe PRIVATE Boost::program_options SystemC::systemc) # ❌ Old way (avoid) include_directories(include) add_executable(my_exe main.cpp utils.cpp) set_property(TARGET my_exe PROPERTY CXX_STANDARD 17) target_link_libraries(my_exe ${Boost_LIBRARIES} ${SystemC_LIBRARIES}) ``` ### Documentation For comprehensive guidelines, see **[doc/cmake-best-practices.md](doc/cmake-best-practices.md)**, which covers: - Target-based commands and visibility specifiers - Imported targets for all dependencies - Source file management with helper scripts - C++ standard configuration - Compile definitions and include directories - Library linking patterns - Special cases and practical examples ### Maintenance Scripts Use `scripts/generate_cmake_sources.sh` to regenerate source file lists after adding or removing source files: ```bash # Regenerate cmake/sources.cmake with categorized source variables ./scripts/generate_cmake_sources.sh ``` This script scans the `src/` directory and generates `cmake/sources.cmake`, which defines shared source variables used by all build targets: - `ALIOTH_CLUSTER_SOURCES` - Cluster module sources - `ALIOTH_CONFIG_SOURCES` - Configuration sources - `ALIOTH_MODEL_SOURCES` - Core model sources (ax46, atomic, d23v, etc.) - `ALIOTH_PLATFORM_IP_SHARED_SOURCES` - Platform IP sources shared by library targets - `ALIOTH_TESTBENCH_SOURCES` - Testbench sources (build_dev only) - `ALIOTH_PLATFORM_IP_INTERNAL_FULL_SOURCES` - Full internal_use sources Then copy the generated content into the corresponding `target_sources()` block in CMakeLists.txt. ## Directory Structure ``` Alioth/ ├── cfg/ # Configuration parameters for modules ├── lib/ # Framework-related files └── src/ ├── main.cpp # Main entry point with top model selection ├── cli.cpp # Configuration and parameter parsing ├── model/ │ ├── interface/ # Interfaces between modules │ ├── tool/ # Common utility functions │ ├── top/ # Different top model combinations │ └── vip/ # Virtual IPs for validation └── sim/ # Simulator components and adapters ``` ## Commit Guidelines ### Format ``` type[scope]: description [optional body] [optional footer] ``` ### Types - aiTitle: Compare Alioth simulation speedup across platforms

content.text:
No published Alioth-vs-others speed numbers in this repo. Below is the industry-typical ordering and rough magnitudes; treat Alioth's row as a ballpark since exact MIPS depends on core variant, MSS detail, and Clarity/log flags.

| Platform | Type | Typical simulated speed | vs Alioth | Timing fidelity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **QEMU (TCG)** | Functional JIT | 200-1000 MIPS | ~1000-10,000x faster | None (functional only) |
| **QEMU (KVM)** | Native virt | ~native (>1000 MIPS) | ~10,000x faster | None |
| **FPGA emulation** | Real RTL on FPGA | 10-100 MHz simulated clock (~10-100 MIPS) | ~100-1000x faster | Cycle-exact (it *is* the RTL) |
| **Alioth (release)** | SystemC cycle-approx + ISS | ~0.1-1 MIPS per core | 1x | Cycle-aligned to RTL, small CPI gap |
| **Verilator (RTL)** | C++ codegen from Verilog | 1-50 kHz simulated clock (~1-50 KIPS for a full SoC) | ~10-100x slower | Cycle-exact (the RTL itself) |

Key takeaways:

- **QEMU** is for *running* the workload, not measuring it. Best for OS boot, functional bring-up, regression. No pipeline/cache timing.
- **Alioth** sits in the cycle-approximate sweet spot: orders of magnitude faster than Verilator while still tracking RTL cycles within a small CPI gap. Slower than QEMU because every cycle is modeled (tick-tock, MSS, ACE, Clarity).
- **Verilator** is the slowest because it simulates *every wire toggle* in software. Only choice when you need bit-exact RTL behavior without FPGA hardware.
- **FPGA** is the fastest cycle-accurate option but needs synthesizable RTL, board bring-up, and debug is far harder than software simulation.

Typical workflow uses all four: QEMU for functional/Linux work -> Alioth for perf evaluation pre-tapeout -> Verilator for RTL regression -> FPGA for long-trace validation and software co-development.

If you want repo-grounded numbers, point me at a speedtest log or `.gitea/workflows/speedtest.yaml` output and I can extract the actual MIPS for the current build.

message.content: from the market requirements document, if Alioth and Verilator are slower than FPGA, why do we need those two tools? explain their usage

content.text:
FPGA is fastest but only exists *late* in the design cycle and gives *poor visibility* — Alioth and Verilator fill the gaps before FPGA is usable and provide observability FPGA can't.

## The 3 tools cover 3 different problems

| Problem | Best tool | Why others fail |
|---|---|---|
| "What should we build?" (sizing caches, vector width, MSHR count before RTL exists) | **Alioth** | FPGA/Verilator need RTL — RTL doesn't exist yet |
| "Is the RTL correct?" (cycle-exact bug hunting, waveform debug) | **Verilator** | FPGA hides signals; Alioth is not the RTL |
| "Does real software run fast enough?" (boot Linux, run weeks of regression) | **FPGA** | Alioth/Verilator too slow for billion-cycle runs |

## Why Alioth, even though it's slower than FPGA

1. **Available 12-18 months before RTL.** Architecture team must decide cache size, vector width, ROB depth *before* anyone writes Verilog. FPGA can't help — no RTL to map.
2. **Customer deliverable.** Andes ships Alioth to customers so they can size their SoC and run their workloads pre-silicon. Customers can't get the FPGA bitstream (IP protection) or wait for tapeout.
3. **Parameter sweeps in minutes.** Change L1 size in YAML, rerun. On FPGA this means re-synthesis + place-and-route (hours per point).
4. **Full observability.** Clarity DB dumps every pipeline event; HPM counters expose every microarchitectural signal. FPGA needs ChipScope/ILA with a tiny capture buffer.
5. **Runs on any laptop.** No board, no license server (mostly), no synthesis tool.

## Why Verilator, even though it's slower than FPGA

1. **Pre-FPGA gate.** You must prove RTL is correct before spending hours synthesizing it. Verilator catches bugs in minutes that would take a full FPGA rebuild to discover.
2. **Every wire visible.** Waveform (FSDB/VCD) shows every signal at every cycle. FPGA ChipScope captures maybe 1024 samples on 32 selected signals.
3. **Reproducible.** Same seed = same waveform = same bug. FPGA timing/async behavior can be hard to reproduce.
4. **Verification testbench (UVM, constrained random, coverage).** The DV flow lives in simulators, not on FPGA.
5. **No hardware cost.** Verilator runs on the same Linux box as everything else. Big emulators (Palladium, ZeBu) cost millions; FPGA dev kits still cost thousands and take weeks to bring up.

## Timeline view

```
Time ------------------------------------------------------------>

[Spec / Architecture]   [RTL Development]   [RTL Verification]   [Pre-silicon SW]   [Silicon]
       Alioth ---->          Alioth +            Verilator -->        FPGA --->
                            Verilator            (gold ref)          (long runs)
   (sweep design,           (compare to        (find RTL bugs,      (boot OS,
    correlate w/ RTL          Alioth)           waveform debug)     run weeks
    once it exists)                                                  of code)
```

## One-line MRD pitch for each

- **Alioth**: *"Pick the right microarchitecture, and let customers measure their workload, before RTL exists."*
- **Verilator**: *"Prove the RTL is correct, with every signal visible, on any Linux box."*
- **FPGA**: *"Run real software at near-real speed once RTL is stable."*

All three are needed because no single tool covers (early availability) + (full visibility) + (high speed) at once. FPGA wins only on speed.

1	# CLAUDE.md
2	
3	This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
4	* Always update docs/USER_GUIDE.md if something changed.
5	
6	## Repository Overview
7	
8	Andes hybrid RISC-V co-simulator: QEMU 9.x (functional, MHz-level) + vsim (SystemC + Verilator, cycle-accurate) share architectural state across a magic-CSR boundary. The system runs a three-phase round-trip: **QEMU1** (drain on CSR/PC trigger) -> **vsim** (resume + execute + drain) -> **QEMU2** (restore via gdbstub, continue).
9	
10	Two Git submodules:
11	- `QEMU/` - QEMU fork hosting the TCG plugin (branch: `hybrid`)
12	- `verilator/` - vsim sources; `hybrid/` subdirs hold the plugin and test fixtures
13	- `tools/simpoint/` - SimPoint 3.2 (UCSD) clustering binary; pinned to upstream `17783e5`
14	
15	Shared ABI lives at `include/hybrid/state_abi.h` (not inside either submodule).
16	
17	## Build Commands
18	
19	**Primary path (`./hsim`)** -- the end-user driver, used in all user-facing docs:
20	
21	```sh
22	./hsim build                       # builds qemu, vsim, plugin, simpoint, fixtures
23	./hsim test                        # full e2e suite (defaults: MODE=both, JOBS=8)
24	./hsim run <elf> --mode csr|pc|icount|slice  # one round-trip
25	./hsim list <fixtures|modes>
26	```
27	
28	**Developer escape hatch** -- the underlying scripts. Use these when
29	working on the build system, the harness, or a single leg in isolation:
30	
31	```sh
32	# Build everything (qemu -> vsim -> plugin -> simpoint)
33	source ./setup.sh
34	
35	# Build individual components
36	./scripts/build_qemu.sh                              # QEMU (configure + make -j64)
37	./scripts/build_vsim.sh                              # vsim (Docker/podman, runs ./build.sh inside container)
38	make -C qemu_plugin QEMU_ROOT=./QEMU  # TCG plugin (out-of-tree)
39	./scripts/build_simpoint.sh                          # SimPoint clustering binary (g++ on host)
40	
41	# Build RISC-V ELF test fixtures
42	make -C tests/fixtures              # all fixtures
43	make -C tests/fixtures rt_c_v_regs.elf  # single fixture
44	
45	# Clean
46	source ./setup.sh clean [qemu|vsim|plugin|simpoint|all]
47	```
48	
49	**Outputs:**
50	- `build/qemu/qemu-system-riscv64`
51	- `verilator/build/sim_ax45mpv_premium` (or other CPU variant)
52	- `qemu_plugin/libhybrid_handoff.so`
53	- `tools/simpoint/bin/simpoint`
54	
55	`scripts/build_vsim.sh` is Docker-based (podman). It builds an image from `verilator/Dockerfile` (target `env`) then runs `./build.sh` inside it, mounting the repo at `/work` and `include/` as `/include:ro`.
56	
57	## Running Tests
58	
59	```sh
60	# All e2e tests in parallel (auto-detects job count from nproc + /dev/shm headroom)
61	bash scripts/run_e2e.sh
62	
63	# Run with specific options
64	JOBS=4 MODE=csr bash scripts/run_e2e.sh         # 4-way parallel, CSR-mode only
65	JOBS=1 bash scripts/run_e2e.sh                  # sequential (debug)
66	FILTER=rt_c_v bash scripts/run_e2e.sh           # regex filter on fixture name
67	LOG_DIR=/tmp/my-logs bash scripts/run_e2e.sh    # custom log directory
68	
69	# Unit tests (inside vsim build container)
70	# The container build runs: cmake --build build -j
71	# To run ctest directly after build:
72	#   podman run ... ./build.sh && podman exec ... ctest --test-dir build -L hybrid-e2e
73	```
74	
75	**Important:** on a high-core-count machine (128+ cores) `default_jobs()` computes `min(nproc, /dev/shm_free/256MB)` which can reach 128+. Running that many vsim Verilator processes simultaneously saturates CPU and causes timeouts. Use `JOBS=8` (or lower) as a practical cap: `JOBS=8 bash scripts/run_e2e.sh`.
76	
77	`scripts/run_e2e.sh` exits 0 only when all tests pass. Logs go to a `mktemp` directory under `/tmp`; path is printed at the start of each run. Each test's full output lands in `$LOG_DIR/$mode--$name.log`.
78	
79	**Manual driver tests**: `tests/hsim/test_hsim_*.sh` are per-feature RED-then-green smoke tests for `./hsim` subcommands (F1..F14). They are run manually during driver development, not wired into `scripts/run_e2e.sh`. Each script is self-contained (sources `setup.sh` artifacts, runs one subcommand, asserts on stdout). The same convention applies to `tests/plugin/test_plugin_*.sh` (QEMU-plugin-only smoke tests).
80	
81	## Architecture
82	
83	### Three-Phase Handoff
84	
85	```
86	QEMU1 --(state file)--> vsim --(state file + V-scratch mmap)--> QEMU2
87	```
88	
89	1. **QEMU plugin** (`qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`) - TCG plugin. On CSR-write trigger (`csrwi 0x7C0, 0`) or PC-trigger, drains QEMU's architectural state into a binary `hybrid_state_v1` struct written to `--outfile`.
90	2. **vsim handoff controller** (`src/hybrid/handoff_controller.hpp`) - Detects the trigger inside vsim, pauses the hart via DMI, then calls `ResumeDriver` to restore state.
91	3. **ResumeDriver** (`src/hybrid/resume_driver.hpp`) - Writes GPRs/FPRs/CSRs/V-state into the vsim hart via RISC-V Debug Module Abstract Commands and Program Buffer.
92	4. **StateDrain** (`src/hybrid/state_drain.hpp`) - On vsim exit trigger, reads back the full architectural state via DMI Abstract Commands.
93	5. **qemu_handback** (`src/hybrid/qemu_handback.hpp`) - Spawns QEMU2, connects via gdbstub, sends P-packet register writes for GPRs/FPRs/CSRs/V-regs, then `continue`s.
94	
95	**CSR restore split**: `ResumeDriver` writes only the CSRs that the vsim phase can touch: `mstatus`, `mtvec`, `mcycle`, `minstret`. The QEMU plugin still drains the full M-mode set (`mepc`, `mcause`, `mtval`, `mscratch`, `medeleg`, `mideleg`, `mip`, `mie`, `satp`) plus PMP (64 `pmpaddr` + 16 `pmpcfg`) into `hybrid_state_v1`, but those are restored only on QEMU2 via the gdbstub P-packet path in `qemu_handback`. The vsim phase is assumed trap-free and PMP-static; if a future workload needs traps or dynamic PMP inside the ROI, `ResumeDriver` must be extended.
96	
97	### Trigger Modes
98	
99	The repo ships 4 switching modes, split by what they profile.
100	
101	Kernel modes (measure one region you choose):
102	- **CSR mode** (default): Pattern-matches `csrwi 0x7C0, 0` (entry) / `csrwi 0x7C0, 1` (exit) at retire time. CSR 0x7C0 is a benign vendor write on Andes ax45mp.
103	- **PC mode**: explicit boundary PCs passed as `--pc-start S --pc-end E` (symbol name or `0x` address) resolved at startup; CSR insns are bypassed. Both args are required.
104	
105	Whole-program modes (sample by instruction count):
106	- **icount mode**: single boundary on each leg - plugin `icount=N` fast-forwards QEMU1, vsim `--hybrid-icount M` measures the window and drains. No markers, no warmup; for CSR-less workloads.
107	- **SimPoint-driven mode**: profile the run into slices (interval = insns per slice), cluster representative phases, measure each phase like icount, weight-combine into a whole-program cycle estimate. Drive via `./hsim run --mode simpoint` (or the equivalent `./hsim estimate`). The bbv-profile / archive / replay machinery are its stages, not separate modes.
108	
109	`./hsim run --mode csr|pc|icount|simpoint` is the unified orchestrator; `tests/e2e.sh` drives csr/pc internally. Each yields a cycle figure: kernel/window cycles = the vsim `mcycle` delta (`hybrid_state_v1::mcycle`); SimPoint reports the weight-combined `estimated_cycles`.
110	
111	### Shared ABI (`include/hybrid/state_abi.h`)
112	
113	`hybrid_state_v1` is the binary wire format exchanged between QEMU plugin, vsim, and the handback path. It holds: 32 GPRs, 32 FPRs, M-mode CSRs (mstatus, mepc, etc.), PMP (64 pmpaddr + 16 pmpcfg), and the V extension block (vstart, vtype, vl, vlenb, 32 vreg[], vxsat, vxrm, vcsr). `HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX=64` supports VLEN up to 512 bits. Multi-byte fields are little-endian (native on RV64 + x86-64 host); the format is not endian-portable.
114	
115	Flags (`HYBRID_FLAG_RV64`, `HYBRID_FLAG_FP`, `HYBRID_FLAG_V`) gate which state blocks are live. The ABI struct is validated by `tests/hybrid/state_abi.test.cpp`.
116	
117	### V-State Transport
118	
119	V data registers (v0..v31) move through a fixed scratch region
120	(`kVScratchGpa = 0x00FF0000` on `-M andes_ae350`) in the shared mmap. vsim drives
121	the transfer via the Debug Module **Program Buffer** while the hart is halted, so
122	benchmark binaries issue no transport code:

144	   overwrites the sweep's vtype/vl/vstart) and uses x5/x6/x7 as scratch.
145	3. `vsetvl x0, x5, x6` in Program Buffer (stages `vl` in x5, `vtype` in x6 via abstract GPR writes first)

151	LAST, after every architectural read (GPRs/FPRs/V-CSRs/mcycle/minstret), so the
152	sweep's clobbers and any counter increments cannot corrupt the drained state.
