## 8. Phase 3 E2E Test Expansion

### 8.1 Context

Phase 3 landed the round-trip mechanism. The existing e2e harness `tests/hybrid/e2e.sh` exercises the full QEMU1 -> vsim -> QEMU2 path but with a single fixture (`handoff_roundtrip.S`) that only validates ONE GPR (`a2 == 3`) via the semihosting exit code. The plumbing works, but two large coverage gaps remain before we move on to Phase 4:

- **Register coverage**: 1 of 31 GPRs is observed; ABI-special regs (`sp`/`gp`/`tp`/`ra`/`fp`) are never touched; sign-bit and full-64-bit values are not exercised; the `HYBRID_HANDOFF_RUNTIME` trigger form (`csrrw rd,0x7C0,rs1`) is never fired in e2e.
- **Memory coverage**: zero tests today. Vsim never executes a load/store between the entry and exit triggers, so the integration of the cache/memory subsystem with the resumed state is unverified. Cross-simulator memory survival via shared mmap is also untested at e2e level (Phase 1 isolated unit test only).

### 8.2 What's actually transferable today (constraints on fixture design)

From `state_drain.hpp:28-45`, `resume_driver.hpp:46-68`, `qemu_handback.hpp:122-144`, `gdbstub_client.hpp:66-82`, and `hybrid_handoff.c:101-124`:

| State class | Fully round-tripped? |
|---|---|
| `x1..x31`, `pc` | yes |
| `priv` | hardcoded to 3 in both directions |
| `f0..f31`, all CSRs (mstatus/mepc/mtvec/...), V regs, PMP | NOT transferred (Phase 5) |
| Memory written in vsim, read in QEMU 2 | NOT transferred unless `--shared-mem-path` is wired into `qemu_handback.hpp` (currently it isn't) |

Implication: every Tier-1 fixture must encode pass/fail into a **GPR before the exit csrwi**, then in the QEMU 2 phase (after the csrwi, where DPC lands) verify and ship the result through `SYS_EXIT_EXTENDED`. We cannot use FP/CSR/V state as test channels yet.

### 8.3 Fixture three-phase template

Every new fixture follows this layout (text base `0x80000000`, semihosting param block at `0x80001000` per the existing convention):

```
_start:                          // PHASE A: runs in QEMU 1 (functional)
    <set up initial state>
    csrwi   0x7C0, 0             // QEMU drains x1..x31+pc, exits

phase_b:                         // PHASE B: runs in vsim (RTL, cycle-accurate)
    <transform state under test>
    csrwi   0x7C0, 1             // vsim drains, exits 200
                                 //   on the way out, main spawns QEMU 2
                                 //   gdbstub restores x1..x31+pc, sends c
phase_c:                         // PHASE C: runs in QEMU 2 (functional)
    <fold result into checksum/bitmask in t2>
    li      t0, 0x80001000       // semihosting param block
    li      t1, 0x20026          // ADP_Stopped_ApplicationExit
    sd      t1, 0(t0)
    sd      t2, 8(t0)            // exit_code = checksum (0 == pass)
    li      a0, 0x20             // SYS_EXIT_EXTENDED
    mv      a1, t0
    .option push; .option norvc
    slli x0,x0,0x1f; ebreak; srai x0,x0,0x7
    .option pop
1:  j 1b
```

The single observable signal remains the QEMU 2 process exit code. Per fixture, the bash driver asserts that code matches an expected value (usually 0).

## 9. Cross-Simulator Shared Memory Redesign (Tier-2 Unblocking)

### 9.1 Context (why we are redesigning)

Section 8.5 promised a Tier-2 e2e that maps the same backing file across QEMU 1, vsim, and QEMU 2. The structural plumbing landed (`spawn_qemu` accepts `shared_mem_path`/`shared_mem_size`, `main.cpp` forwards both) but the test fails at vsim startup with:

```
[critical] fatal exception: SimpleMemory external_buffer smaller than region size
```

Root cause is a layout mismatch between vsim's "RAM is everything from 0" model and QEMU's "RAM starts at 0x80000000" model:

| | RAM region | data[0] = GPA | GPA 0x80010000 lands at file offset |
|---|---|---|---|
| vsim main_memory (today) | [0x0, 0x8FFFFFFF] = 2.25 GB (`memory_map.h:8-9`, `platform.hpp:74`) | 0x0 | 0x80010000 |
| QEMU virt machine | [0x80000000, 0x80000000+N) (`qemu_v5/hw/riscv/virt.c` VIRT_DRAM=0x80000000) | 0x80000000 | 0x10000 |

Two derived symptoms:
- `simple_memory.hpp:60-70` rejects external buffers smaller than the full 2.25 GB region, so any non-trivial mmap size fails before bytes are exchanged.
- `simulator.hpp:246` calls `read_elf_into_memory(*elf, xlen_t{0}, ...)` with a hardcoded base of 0; correctness depends on `region.base_address == 0`.

The intended outcome of this redesign: vsim and QEMU agree on which file byte backs which GPA, with no extra owned storage, and with the cycle-accurate path unchanged in non-hybrid mode.

### 9.2 Design (correctness first, then configurable)

**Principle**: in hybrid mode the mmap window IS the addressable RAM. The vsim `main_memory` region is narrowed at construction time to `[base_gpa, base_gpa + size)` where `base_gpa` matches QEMU virt's RAM base (0x80000000). No new "data origin within a wider region" abstraction; the region itself moves.

```
NON-HYBRID (preserved verbatim - default constructor path)
  Platform(ram_buffer = {})
    region        = [RAM_BASE = 0x0, RAM_END = 0x8FFFFFFF]   // 2.25 GB
    storage       = owned vector, 2.25 GB
    ELF load base = region.base_address = 0x0
    ELF segment at 0x80000000 -> data[0x80000000]            // works as today

HYBRID (--shared-mem-path P --shared-mem-size N [--shared-mem-base B = 0x80000000])
  MmapBacking mmap(P, N, base_gpa = B)
  Platform(ram_buffer = mmap.span(), ram_region = [B, B + N - 1])
    region        = [B, B + N - 1]                            // narrow window
    storage       = external mmap span, exactly N bytes       // size check passes
    ELF load base = region.base_address = B = 0x80000000
    ELF segment at 0x80000000 -> data[0]                      // file offset 0
    GPA 0x80010000 -> data[0x10000] = file offset 0x10000     // matches QEMU
    Alias region narrowed to {0,0} (degenerate -> contains() always false)
```

`--shared-mem-base` defaults to 0x80000000 so plain `--shared-mem-path X --shared-mem-size N` Just Works. The flag exists so that future QEMU machine types or alternate test harnesses can override without code changes — this is the "configurable" half of the requirement.

**Alternative considered and rejected**: keep the wide [0, 2.25 GB) region and add a `data_origin` field plus owned-fallback for non-mapped GPAs. Rejected because (a) hybrid mode never needs RAM outside the mmap window — anything below 0x80000000 in QEMU virt is MMIO/ROM, not RAM, and accessing it from vsim while purporting to share with QEMU is already undefined; (b) a sub-range data window doubles the SimpleMemory state machine (mapped vs owned per access); (c) it conflicts with the existing "external_buffer must cover the whole region" contract that other call sites rely on.

aiTitle: Compare Alioth simulation speedup across platforms

content.text:
Yes - hybrid_sim plugs a real gap that *neither* Alioth nor pure Verilator/FPGA covers: **"I want cycle-accurate measurement of a small kernel, but the workload spends 99% of cycles in boring setup."**

## What hybrid_sim actually is

`QEMU 9.x` (functional, ~1000 MIPS) + `vsim` (Verilator-based RTL sim, ~5-9 KHz) sharing memory via `/dev/shm` mmap, switching at a magic CSR / PC / icount / SimPoint trigger. Architectural state moves through a packed C struct (`hybrid_state_v1`); microarch state (caches, BPU, TLB) is discarded - cold start in vsim, optionally warmed up.

Quoting `hybrid_plan.md`: target speedup is **100x-1000x wall-clock reduction** for workloads where the ROI is <1% of dynamic instructions.

## Market gaps it addresses

| Market Requirement | Today's pain | Hybrid_sim answer |
|---|---|---|
| **MR-A**: Measure a benchmark kernel inside a Linux app pre-silicon | Verilator/Alioth too slow to boot Linux; FPGA loses visibility | QEMU boots Linux (minutes), vsim measures the kernel cycle-exact |
| **MR-B**: SPEC-like workloads with long warmup | Cycle-accurate from `_start` to inner loop = days/weeks | SimPoint mode samples representative phases, weight-combines to whole-program CPI |
| **MR-C**: Customer running their own ELF on Andes IP | Customer wait time blocks adoption | ROI-only cycle-accurate, rest of workload at QEMU speed |
| **MR-D**: Iterative microarch tweak + re-measure on real workload | Re-run hours of boot per iteration | Re-measure ROI in minutes; boot once, snapshot, re-enter |
| **MR-E**: Recording kanata/pipeline traces for a steady-state loop | Trace file dominated by boring boot data | Trace exactly the iterations you care about |

This is essentially the **gem5 KVM->O3 switching pattern** that the Alioth-vs-gem5 doc explicitly calls out as missing from Alioth: *"Mid-sim CPU swap: Not supported"*.

## Market gaps it does NOT address

| MR | Why hybrid_sim doesn't help |
|---|---|
| Pre-RTL architecture exploration (cache sizing, vector width) | QEMU has no microarch; you need Alioth alone here |
| Finding RTL bugs in non-ROI code | Bug might be in the boring 99% that runs in QEMU |
| Full Linux regression at near-real speed | FPGA is still better for billions of cycles |
| Functional bring-up | QEMU alone already covers this |

## Where it fits in the 4-tool stack

```
Time --------------------------------------------------->
[Spec]      [RTL Dev]       [Pre-silicon perf eval]      [Late SW dev]
Alioth      Verilator       Alioth + Verilator           FPGA
                            + hybrid_sim (new!)

                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                            covers the workloads
                            previously stuck on
                            "too slow for Verilator,
                             too late for FPGA,
                             too detailed for Alioth-only"
```

## Honest caveats from the repo's own `limitation.md` / `commercial_v1_roadmap.md`

The v1 ROI envelope today is narrow (`docs/limitation.md` core rule):
- **M-mode only**, no S/U-mode (L6)
- **No paging** (satp ignored, L3)
- **Trap-free** in ROI (L4)
- **No syscalls/semihosting** in ROI (L1, **blocker**)
- **No PMP enforcement** in ROI (L2)
- **Single hart** (L8)
- **No Andes vendor CSRs** (L21)
- Hard-wired to `andes_ae350` + `ax45mpv` (L10)

The `commercial_v1_roadmap.md` is a 7-8 month, 6-wave plan to lift those limits from "4/10 commercial" to "8/10". MR-A (Linux-app ROI) only becomes real after **Wave 2** (~18 weeks: S-mode + paging + traps + syscalls).

## The bigger MR question: should there be a QEMU+Alioth hybrid?

Current hybrid_sim is QEMU + **vsim (Verilator)**. The same technology applied to QEMU + **Alioth** would solve a different MR:

| | What you get | Wall-clock for "boot Linux + measure kernel" |
|---|---|---|
| Alioth alone | RTL-correlated CPI | hours-days |
| Verilator alone | Cycle-exact RTL | days-weeks |
| QEMU + vsim (today) | Cycle-exact RTL on ROI | minutes |
| **QEMU + Alioth (hypothetical)** | RTL-correlated CPI on ROI | **minutes**, while keeping Alioth's full visibility (Clarity DB, HPM counters, customer-facing config) |

Customer pitch for QEMU+Alioth: *"Ship Alioth to customers, let them run their Linux apps, get RTL-correlated CPI in minutes instead of days, without needing FPGA hardware or RTL access."*

The handoff ABI, mmap RAM trick, SimPoint clustering, and trigger machinery in hybrid_sim are all simulator-agnostic at the architectural level. Porting the consumer side from vsim to Alioth would mostly be a new `ResumeDriver`/`StateDrain` that drives `afw::Module` state instead of DMI Abstract Commands. The QEMU plugin, wire format, orchestrator, and SimPoint stay the same.

## Recommendation framing for the MRD

**Short answer**: hybrid_sim is solving a *real* MR that the existing tool stack genuinely misses (mid-sim CPU swap, fast-forward boring code, ROI-only cycle accuracy). The MRD case is strongest for **MR-A** (Linux-app kernels) and **MR-B** (SimPoint/SPEC). The v1 envelope is too narrow today to claim those wins, but the commercial roadmap explicitly targets them in ~18-30 weeks. The strategic upside is generalizing the same architecture to **QEMU+Alioth**, which would give Andes a customer-shippable fast-forward story that matches gem5's switching capability while keeping Alioth's RTL-correlation advantage.

# Hybrid Simulator - Market Requirements Document

Status: draft v0.1. Written 2026-05-28. Owner: Nick.

Companion to `commercial_v1_roadmap.md` (engineering plan) and
`limitation.md` (current ROI envelope). This file is the *product*
view: who needs this, why the existing tool stack does not serve
them, and what we must deliver to claim the market.

---

## 1. Problem statement

Pre-silicon performance evaluation today forces customers to pick
exactly one trade-off:

- **QEMU**: runs at MHz, but tells you nothing about cycles.
- **Alioth (SystemC cycle-correlated)**: ~0.1-1 MIPS. Customer-facing,
  RTL-correlated. Booting Linux to a SPEC kernel takes hours-days.
- **Verilator (RTL cycle-exact)**: ~5-9 KHz on Andes RISC-V. Cannot
  reach a real workload's steady state in human time.
- **FPGA / emulator**: near-real speed, cycle-exact, but late in the
  schedule, expensive, and has almost no signal visibility.

The single biggest gap: **"I want cycle-accurate measurement of a
small kernel, but the workload spends 99% of cycles in boring boot,
libc init, OS warmup, and dataset load."** No tool above answers
this without weeks of runtime or a tape-out.

Hybrid simulator closes this gap by running the boring 99% in QEMU
and switching into a cycle-accurate simulator only for the
region of interest (ROI).

---

## 2. Target users

| User | Today's pain | Hybrid_sim payoff |
|---|---|---|
| **Andes architect** evaluating a microarch change on a real workload | Re-runs full Verilator/Alioth for every tweak (days per iteration) | Boot once, re-measure ROI in minutes (100x-1000x faster iteration) |
| **Andes customer** sizing a SoC for their own workload | Cannot wait days; cannot get FPGA before tape-out | Ships hybrid_sim, runs their ELF, gets cycle figures in minutes |
| **SPEC / benchmark engineer** producing whole-program CPI | Fully cycle-accurate run is intractable | SimPoint clustering + per-phase cycle-exact measurement + weighted combine |
| **Pipeline / kanata trace consumer** | Trace file dominated by uninteresting boot | Record only the loop iterations that matter, byte-identical to a fully-RTL baseline |
| **DV engineer** chasing a perf anomaly that only appears after long warmup | Cannot reproduce in Verilator alone | Fast-forward in QEMU to the anomaly, then cycle-exact from there |

---

## 3. Market Requirements

Numbered for traceability into the engineering roadmap.

### MR-A - Linux-userspace ROI measurement

A user shall be able to boot Linux (or any S/U-mode workload), reach
an application's hot loop, hand off to the cycle-accurate simulator,
measure the loop, and hand back.

- **Status**: blocked. ROI is M-mode only today (`limitation.md` core
  rule). Requires Wave 2 of `commercial_v1_roadmap.md`: paging (L3),
  trap state (L4), priv restore (L6), PMP (L2), syscalls in ROI (L1).
- **Acceptance**: a fixture that boots Linux, runs a userspace
  benchmark kernel, returns a cycle count that agrees with a
  fully-RTL baseline within an explicit error budget.

### MR-B - Whole-program estimate via SimPoint

A user shall be able to point hybrid_sim at a long workload and
receive a weighted whole-program cycle estimate without running the
whole workload cycle-accurate.

- **Status**: shipped at v0.x for M-mode workloads (`./hsim run
  --mode simpoint`); `commercial_v1_roadmap.md` Wave 5 (L14) adds
  CI bands and tuned warmup.
- **Acceptance**: estimate within 5-10% of fully-RTL for at least 3
  SPEC-class workloads.

### MR-C - Customer-deliverable workload measurement

An Andes customer with their own ELF shall be able to run that ELF
against hybrid_sim and get RTL-correlated cycle figures, without
needing FPGA hardware or RTL access.

- **Status**: blocked on MR-A plus Andes vendor CSR parity
  (`commercial_v1_roadmap.md` Wave 3, L21) and trigger redesign
  (L12 - move off CSR `0x7C0`).
- **Acceptance**: a customer-style benchmark (closed-source ELF,
  Linux userspace, vendor-CSR usage) round-trips and produces a
  cycle count.

### MR-D - Iterative microarch tweak loop

An architect shall be able to change a microarch parameter, rebuild
the cycle-accurate simulator, and re-measure the same ROI without
re-running the boot phase.

- **Status**: partially supported (QEMU phase is stable; vsim
  rebuild is independent). Wider envelope (MR-A) makes this usable
  on real workloads.
- **Acceptance**: edit-rebuild-measure cycle under 5 minutes for a
  kernel inside a Linux app.

### MR-E - ROI-only pipeline trace recording

A user shall be able to record kanata or Clarity-style pipeline
traces for exactly the iterations of interest, with byte-identical
output to a fully-RTL baseline over that window.

- **Status**: shipped at v0.x for M-mode (kanata integration in
  Phase 4 of `hybrid_plan.md`).
- **Acceptance**: kanata diff is empty against a fully-RTL baseline
  for the recorded window after warmup.

---

## 4. Competitive positioning

Single-tool view:

| Tool | Speed (rough) | Cycle fidelity | Visibility | Available |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| QEMU (TCG) | 200-1000 MIPS | none | low | always |
| Alioth | 0.1-1 MIPS | RTL-correlated, small CPI gap | high (Clarity DB, HPM) | post pipeline model |
| Verilator | 1-50 KHz | cycle-exact (is the RTL) | very high (every wire) | when RTL exists |
| FPGA | 10-100 MHz | cycle-exact | very low (ILA only) | very late |
| **Hybrid_sim (QEMU + vsim)** | QEMU speed for boring code, vsim speed in ROI | cycle-exact in ROI | very high in ROI | needs RTL for vsim leg |

The pitch is *not* "faster than FPGA". It is **"the only tool that
gives Verilator-grade fidelity on a kernel inside a workload that is
too long for Verilator to reach"**. That is a different axis.

---

## 5. Where hybrid_sim does NOT help

Honest scope-out, to keep the MRD credible:

- **Pre-RTL architecture exploration** (cache sizing, vector width,
  ROB depth before any RTL exists). Use Alioth alone.
- **RTL bug hunting outside the ROI**. If the bug is in boot or
  setup code, hybrid_sim runs that part on QEMU and never exercises
  the RTL there.
- **Full-system regression at near-real speed**. Use FPGA.
- **Functional bring-up of a new core**. Use QEMU alone.
- **Workloads with no clear ROI** (e.g. a long random benchmark
  with no hot kernel). SimPoint mode mitigates but cannot eliminate
  the problem.

---

## 6. v1 envelope vs market reach

Today's narrow envelope (from `limitation.md`):

- M-mode only, no S/U-mode (L6)
- No virtual memory (L3)
- Trap-free ROI (L4)
- No syscalls / semihosting in ROI (L1, blocker)
- No PMP enforcement (L2)
- Single hart (L8)
- No Andes vendor CSRs (L21)
- Hard-wired to `andes_ae350` + `ax45mpv` (L10)

Implication: **MR-A, MR-C, MR-D cannot ship today.** Only MR-B (in
M-mode workloads) and MR-E (in M-mode workloads) are claimable.

Ship targets (from `commercial_v1_roadmap.md`):

| Milestone | Cumulative weeks | MRs claimable |
|---|---|---|
| Wave 0 + Wave 1 | 6 | MR-B (M-mode), MR-E (M-mode) - same as today, but loud about wrongness |
| MV beta (Wave 0+1 + L3+L4+L6) | ~18 | MR-A partial (S-mode, traps, paging), MR-B widened |
| Commercial v1.0 (Waves 0-5) | ~30 | MR-A, MR-B, MR-C, MR-D, MR-E |

---

## 7. Success metrics

How we know hybrid_sim is winning its market:

1. **Wall-clock speedup**: on a representative workload with ROI <
   1% of dynamic instructions, hybrid_sim produces a cycle figure at
   least **100x faster** than vsim-alone. Target stretch: 1000x.
2. **Accuracy**: per-ROI cycle figure within **<= 1%** of a fully-RTL
   baseline (excluding the documented microarch warm-up discontinuity).
3. **Whole-program estimate**: SimPoint output within **5-10%** of
   fully-RTL on at least 3 SPEC-class workloads.
4. **Customer adoption**: at least one external customer running
   their own ELF end-to-end under hybrid_sim.
5. **Time-to-first-result**: a new user goes from `git clone` to a
   working round-trip cycle figure in **under 30 minutes**.

---

## 8. Future direction - QEMU + Alioth

The hybrid_sim architecture is *consumer-agnostic* at the boundary:
QEMU plugin drains state into `hybrid_state_v1`, the consumer
restores it. Today the consumer is vsim (Verilator). A natural
extension is **QEMU + Alioth**.

Comparative pitch:

| Stack | Boot Linux + measure kernel | Visibility | Customer-shippable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alioth alone | hours-days | high | yes |
| QEMU + vsim (today) | minutes | very high | no (vsim needs RTL) |
| **QEMU + Alioth (future)** | **minutes** | **high (Clarity DB, HPM, customer config)** | **yes** |

Strategic case: this would give Andes a customer-shippable
fast-forward story matching gem5's KVM->O3 switching, while
keeping Alioth's RTL-correlation and customer-config advantages.
The Alioth-vs-gem5 doc explicitly calls out
*"Mid-sim CPU swap: Not supported"* as an Alioth gap.

Engineering scope (rough): port the consumer side from DMI Abstract
Commands to `afw::Module` state writes. Everything else - QEMU
plugin, wire format, mmap RAM, SimPoint clustering, orchestrator -
stays the same.

This is NOT scoped into commercial v1.0. It is documented here to
keep the MRD honest about where the platform can go after v1.0.

---

## 9. Open product questions

For PM / lead review:

- **Customer license model**: does hybrid_sim ship inside the same
  customer-facing Alioth bundle, or as a separate add-on?
- **QEMU dependency**: customers run on whatever QEMU we tell them
  to. Do we fork (long-term maintenance) or pin to upstream
  (compatibility risk)?
- **Closed-source customer ELFs**: does the magic-CSR trigger
  approach require customer-source modification, or does PC-trigger
  mode (no source change) cover the common case?
- **Andes vendor CSR exposure**: which Andes-custom CSRs are
  customer-visible and must round-trip? L21 lists 9; do we need
  more?
- **Multi-hart priority**: which customers are blocked on multi-hart
  (L8 / Wave 4)? If none yet, defer beyond v1.0.

---

## 10. References

- `commercial_v1_roadmap.md` - engineering plan, 6 waves, 21
  numbered limitations closed.
- `docs/limitation.md` - current ROI envelope, ground truth.
- `docs/USER_GUIDE.md` - user-facing workflows and modes.
- `hybrid_plan.md` - original design rationale and phased delivery.
- `specs/hybrid-sim-gem5-switch-parity.md` - parity analysis with
  gem5's switchable-CPU mechanism.
- Alioth: `~/work/Alioth/doc/alioth-vs-gem5.md` for the
  "Mid-sim CPU swap: Not supported" gap that QEMU+Alioth would
  close.

- **Acceptance**: a customer-style benchmark (closed-source ELF,
  Linux userspace, vendor-CSR usage) round-trips and produces a
  cycle count.

### MR-D - Iterative microarch tweak loop

An architect shall be able to change a microarch parameter, rebuild
the cycle-accurate simulator, and re-measure the same ROI without
re-running the boot phase.

- **Status**: partially supported (QEMU phase is stable; vsim
  rebuild is independent). Wider envelope (MR-A) makes this usable
  on real workloads.
- **Acceptance**: edit-rebuild-measure cycle under 5 minutes for a
  kernel inside a Linux app.

### MR-E - ROI-only pipeline trace recording

A user shall be able to record kanata or Clarity-style pipeline
traces for exactly the iterations of interest, with byte-identical
output to a fully-RTL baseline over that window.

- **Status**: shipped at v0.x for M-mode (kanata integration in
  Phase 4 of `hybrid_plan.md`).
- **Acceptance**: kanata diff is empty against a fully-RTL baseline
  for the recorded window after warmup.

---

## 4. Competitive positioning

Single-tool view:

| Tool | Speed (rough) | Cycle fidelity | Visibility | Available |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| QEMU (TCG) | 200-1000 MIPS | none | low | always |
| Alioth | 0.1-1 MIPS | RTL-correlated, small CPI gap | high (Clarity DB, HPM) | post pipeline model |
| Verilator | 1-50 KHz | cycle-exact (is the RTL) | very high (every wire) | when RTL exists |
| FPGA | 10-100 MHz | cycle-exact | very low (ILA only) | very late |
| **Hybrid_sim (QEMU + vsim)** | QEMU speed for boring code, vsim speed in ROI | cycle-exact in ROI | very high in ROI | needs RTL for vsim leg |

The pitch is *not* "faster than FPGA". It is **"the only tool that
gives Verilator-grade fidelity on a kernel inside a workload that is
too long for Verilator to reach"**. That is a different axis.

---

## 5. Where hybrid_sim does NOT help

Honest scope-out, to keep the MRD credible:

- **Pre-RTL architecture exploration** (cache sizing, vector width,
  ROB depth before any RTL exists). Use Alioth alone.
- **RTL bug hunting outside the ROI**. If the bug is in boot or
  setup code, hybrid_sim runs that part on QEMU and never exercises
  the RTL there.
- **Full-system regression at near-real speed**. Use FPGA.
- **Functional bring-up of a new core**. Use QEMU alone.
- **Workloads with no clear ROI** (e.g. a long random benchmark
  with no hot kernel). SimPoint mode mitigates but cannot eliminate
  the problem.

---

## 6. v1 envelope vs market reach

Today's narrow envelope (from `limitation.md`):

- M-mode only, no S/U-mode (L6)
- No virtual memory (L3)
- Trap-free ROI (L4)
- No syscalls / semihosting in ROI (L1, blocker)
- No PMP enforcement (L2)
- Single hart (L8)
- No Andes vendor CSRs (L21)
- Hard-wired to `andes_ae350` + `ax45mpv` (L10)

Implication: **MR-A, MR-C, MR-D cannot ship today.** Only MR-B (in
M-mode workloads) and MR-E (in M-mode workloads) are claimable.

Ship targets (from `commercial_v1_roadmap.md`):

| Milestone | Cumulative weeks | MRs claimable |
|---|---|---|
| Wave 0 + Wave 1 | 6 | MR-B (M-mode), MR-E (M-mode) - same as today, but loud about wrongness |
| MV beta (Wave 0+1 + L3+L4+L6) | ~18 | MR-A partial (S-mode, traps, paging), MR-B widened |
| Commercial v1.0 (Waves 0-5) | ~30 | MR-A, MR-B, MR-C, MR-D, MR-E |

---

## 7. Success metrics

How we know hybrid_sim is winning its market:

1. **Wall-clock speedup**: on a representative workload with ROI <
   1% of dynamic instructions, hybrid_sim produces a cycle figure at
   least **100x faster** than vsim-alone. Target stretch: 1000x.
2. **Accuracy**: per-ROI cycle figure within **<= 1%** of a fully-RTL
   baseline (excluding the documented microarch warm-up discontinuity).
3. **Whole-program estimate**: SimPoint output within **5-10%** of
   fully-RTL on at least 3 SPEC-class workloads.
4. **Customer adoption**: at least one external customer running
   their own ELF end-to-end under hybrid_sim.
5. **Time-to-first-result**: a new user goes from `git clone` to a
   working round-trip cycle figure in **under 30 minutes**.

---

## 8. Future direction - QEMU + Alioth

The hybrid_sim architecture is *consumer-agnostic* at the boundary:
QEMU plugin drains state into `hybrid_state_v1`, the consumer
restores it. Today the consumer is vsim (Verilator). A natural
extension is **QEMU + Alioth**.

Comparative pitch:

| Stack | Boot Linux + measure kernel | Visibility | Customer-shippable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alioth alone | hours-days | high | yes |
| QEMU + vsim (today) | minutes | very high | no (vsim needs RTL) |
| **QEMU + Alioth (future)** | **minutes** | **high (Clarity DB, HPM, customer config)** | **yes** |

Strategic case: this would give Andes a customer-shippable
fast-forward story matching gem5's KVM->O3 switching, while
keeping Alioth's RTL-correlation and customer-config advantages.
The Alioth-vs-gem5 doc explicitly calls out
*"Mid-sim CPU swap: Not supported"* as an Alioth gap.

Engineering scope (rough): port the consumer side from DMI Abstract
Commands to `afw::Module` state writes. Everything else - QEMU
plugin, wire format, mmap RAM, SimPoint clustering, orchestrator -
stays the same.

This is NOT scoped into commercial v1.0. It is documented here to
keep the MRD honest about where the platform can go after v1.0.

---

## 9. Open product questions

For PM / lead review:

- **Customer license model**: does hybrid_sim ship inside the same
  customer-facing Alioth bundle, or as a separate add-on?
- **QEMU dependency**: customers run on whatever QEMU we tell them
  to. Do we fork (long-term maintenance) or pin to upstream
  (compatibility risk)?
- **Closed-source customer ELFs**: does the magic-CSR trigger
  approach require customer-source modification, or does PC-trigger
  mode (no source change) cover the common case?
- **Andes vendor CSR exposure**: which Andes-custom CSRs are
  customer-visible and must round-trip? L21 lists 9; do we need
  more?
- **Multi-hart priority**: which customers are blocked on multi-hart
  (L8 / Wave 4)? If none yet, defer beyond v1.0.

---

## 10. References

- `commercial_v1_roadmap.md` - engineering plan, 6 waves, 21
  numbered limitations closed.
- `docs/limitation.md` - current ROI envelope, ground truth.
- `docs/USER_GUIDE.md` - user-facing workflows and modes.
- `hybrid_plan.md` - original design rationale and phased delivery.
- `specs/hybrid-sim-gem5-switch-parity.md` - parity analysis with
  gem5's switchable-CPU mechanism.
- Alioth: `~/work/Alioth/doc/alioth-vs-gem5.md` for the
  "Mid-sim CPU swap: Not supported" gap that QEMU+Alioth would
  close.

message.content: I don't understand why you propose QEMU+Alioth, compare against QEMU+verilator

content.text:
Fair pushback. The honest comparison:

## They serve different markets, not the same one

| Axis | QEMU + vsim (today) | QEMU + Alioth (proposed) |
|---|---|---|
| **Customer-shippable?** | **NO** - vsim runs the real RTL, RTL is IP | **YES** - Alioth is already the customer-facing model |
| **Available pre-RTL?** | NO - vsim needs RTL to exist | YES - Alioth exists 12-18 months before RTL |
| **Speed in ROI** | 5-9 KHz simulated clock (~5-9 KIPS) | 0.1-1 MIPS (~100x faster than vsim in ROI) |
| **CPI fidelity** | cycle-exact (IS the RTL) | RTL-correlated, small CPI gap |
| **Output** | every wire, FSDB, kanata | Clarity DB, HPM counters (internal + external), customer-facing |
| **Build iteration** | hours (Verilator translate) | minutes (SystemC rebuild) |
| **Long-ROI tractability** | poor (5-9 KHz dies on million-cycle kernels) | better (100x headroom) |
| **Audience** | Andes internal DV / arch team | Andes customers + arch team |

## The single biggest differentiator: who can run it

QEMU + vsim **cannot ship to customers** because vsim contains the actual Verilog. The whole hybrid_sim repo today is an *internal* tool.

QEMU + Alioth would be the *customer-shippable* version of the same idea. Andes already ships Alioth to customers (per the alioth-vs-gem5 doc: "Audience: IP designers + customers correlating with RTL"). Adding a QEMU front-end is the only way to give customers a "fast-forward to my kernel" story without handing them the RTL.

## Honest case AGAINST building QEMU + Alioth

Three things must all be true for the investment to pay off:

1. **Customers actually need Linux-bearing workloads** measured pre-silicon (not just bare-metal kernels).
2. **They can't wait hours-days** for Alioth alone (Alioth is already 100x-1000x faster than vsim - is another 100x from QEMU fast-forward really needed?).
3. **They have no RTL access**, so QEMU + vsim is closed to them.

If any one is false, the existing stack works:
- Andes internal teams -> QEMU + vsim (have RTL, need cycle-exact)
- Customers with small bare-metal kernels -> Alioth alone (already fast enough)
- Customers with no perf-measurement need -> QEMU alone (functional)

## Where each one wins (decision matrix)

| Use case | Best tool |
|---|---|
| Pipeline waveform forensics on a small kernel | QEMU + vsim (need every wire) |
| Cycle-exact sign-off pre-tapeout | QEMU + vsim (need bit-exact) |
| RTL bug hunt that only appears after long warmup | QEMU + vsim |
| Customer measures their Linux app on Andes IP | QEMU + Alioth (only option - no RTL access) |
| Pre-RTL architecture exploration on a real benchmark | QEMU + Alioth (RTL doesn't exist yet) |
| Architect sweeps cache size on 10 workloads | QEMU + Alioth (100x faster iteration than vsim) |
| Customer wants HPM-counter view, not wire-level | QEMU + Alioth (Clarity DB + HPM is the customer API) |

## My honest recommendation

QEMU + Alioth is worth building **only if** the product team confirms #1 above - that customers want Linux-userspace workloads measured pre-silicon. If customer demand is "bare-metal kernels under 1B cycles", Alioth alone covers it and QEMU + Alioth is dead weight.

Want me to:
- (a) revise MRD Section 8 to make this customer-vs-internal split explicit, or
- (b) drop Section 8 entirely until the product team confirms the customer-Linux demand?

content.text:
Closest commercial competitors, ordered by directness of fit:

## Tier 1 - Direct equivalents (high-end EDA)

| Tool | Fast side | Cycle side | Hybrid mechanism | Price tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Synopsys ZeBu + Virtualizer** | Virtualizer (SystemC TLM, MHz) | ZeBu FPGA emulator | Transactor-based handoff | $$$ M+ capex + maintenance |
| **Cadence Palladium + Helium** | Helium virtual platform | Palladium Z2 emulator | "Dynamic Duo" / Hybrid Verification Flow | $$$ M+ capex |
| **Siemens (Mentor) Veloce + Vista** | Vista virtual prototyping | Veloce Strato emulator | Veloce HYCON | $$$ M+ capex |

These are the canonical "boot Linux in TLM, switch to cycle-accurate emulator at the ROI" tools. Used by big SoC vendors (Apple, Qualcomm, Intel, AMD). The exact pattern hybrid_sim implements, but with a multi-million-dollar emulator on the cycle side instead of a Verilator software sim.

## Tier 2 - RISC-V mid-tier

| Tool | Fast side | Cycle side | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Synopsys Imperas** (formerly Imperas, acquired ~2024) | OVPsim (functional) | Imperas timing-extension models, can drive RTL via DPI | The dominant commercial RISC-V hybrid story; many RISC-V vendors used Imperas before Synopsys bought them |
| **ARM Fast Models + Cycle Models** | Fast Models (MIPS-class) | Cycle Models (cycle-accurate) | ARM-only, not directly RISC-V, but the swap pattern is identical |
| **Wind River Simics** | Full-system functional | "Hindsight" cycle analysis | Intel-owned, full-system Linux focus, less RTL-correlation |

## Tier 3 - Open / academic

| Tool | Fast side | Cycle side | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **gem5 KVM -> O3CPU swap** | KVM (native virt) or AtomicSimpleCPU | O3CPU | Open source. The reference pattern hybrid_sim follows |
| **Spike + RTL co-sim bridges** (various) | Spike (functional ISS) | DPI/RTL | Hobby/academic; no productized hybrid |

## How hybrid_sim positions against them

| Dimension | ZeBu/Palladium hybrid | Imperas hybrid | hybrid_sim |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost | $M+ capex | $K-M license | $0 (internal) |
| Cycle-side | FPGA emulator (10-100 MHz) | DPI to RTL sim | Verilator (5-9 KHz) |
| Speed in ROI | very high | medium | low |
| RTL needed | yes | yes | yes (vsim leg) |
| Customer-shippable | yes (some) | yes | no (vsim has Andes RTL) |
| RISC-V native | retrofit | yes | yes |
| Andes IP support | generic | generic | first-class |

## Competitive niche for hybrid_sim

**Where it wins** against the commercial alternatives:
- **Cost**: $0 vs $M+ for ZeBu/Palladium. Andes engineers and customers pay zero per-seat.
- **Andes-specific**: first-class support for Andes vendor CSRs, ACE, ax45/ax46/ax50/d23v variants, kanata/Clarity output. Generic tools don't know about these.
- **Pre-tape-out access**: no FPGA bring-up wait; runs on any Linux box.

**Where it loses**:
- **Speed on the cycle side**: ZeBu/Palladium do 10-100 MHz, hybrid_sim's vsim does 5-9 KHz. ~10,000x gap.
- **OS-bearing workloads**: ZeBu hybrid boots Linux for real; hybrid_sim is M-mode-only today (Wave 2 of the roadmap closes this).
- **Maturity**: ZeBu/Palladium are 10+ years productized; hybrid_sim is alpha.

## Implication for MRD

The commercial alternatives prove the **pattern has a market** - if it didn't, Synopsys/Cadence/Siemens wouldn't sell million-dollar tools for it. Hybrid_sim's wedge is *not* "we do this pattern better than ZeBu" - it's:

> "We do the pattern at $0 cost, with Andes IP support out of the box, for the customer tier that cannot afford a $5M emulator."

That is the right competitive framing for the MRD. The risk: if a customer can afford ZeBu and already has it, they will not pick hybrid_sim. The target customer is the **mid-tier RISC-V SoC integrator** who needs perf data but cannot justify Tier-1 emulator capex.

  need a board and weeks of partitioning per design point.
- **Customer-shippable** (with QEMU + Alioth path, Section 8):

  is M-mode-only until Wave 2 of the roadmap closes L1-L6.
- **Maturity**: ZeBu/Palladium are 10+ years productized with full

- **Generic ISA / SoC coverage**: ZeBu/Palladium are ISA-agnostic
  and customer-configurable; hybrid_sim is hard-wired to
  `andes_ae350` + `ax45mpv` until L10 closes.

### 9.4 Target customer profile

The commercial alternatives delineate the addressable market.
Hybrid_sim's most likely customer:

- Mid-tier RISC-V SoC integrator with an Andes IP license.
- Cannot justify $M+ ZeBu/Palladium capex.
- Has perf-measurement needs beyond what QEMU alone provides.
- Today: bare-metal kernels. Wave 2 onward: Linux userspace.
- Wants Andes-correlated CPI figures, not generic numbers.

The customer who **can** afford ZeBu **and** needs full-system Linux
at emulator speed is **not** our target. We compete in the tier
below.

### 9.5 Risks from the commercial landscape

- **Tier-1 price compression**: Synopsys / Cadence may discount
  hybrid solutions for RISC-V mid-tier customers; our cost wedge
  narrows.
- **Imperas under Synopsys**: now part of a Tier-1 vendor; may
  expand into Andes IP support. Monitor.
- **Customer-built in-house tools**: SiFive, MIPS, others may build
  similar internally. IP defensibility is weak; speed of delivery
  matters.
- **gem5 productization** (low probability): if a vendor
  productizes gem5 hybrid with RISC-V support, our open-source /
  cost story weakens.

Added Section 9 "Competitive landscape" with 5 subsections (competitor matrix, win cases, lose cases, target customer profile, market risks). Renumbered Open product questions to 10, References to 11.

Summary of new content:

- **9.1** - 3-tier matrix: Tier 1 ZeBu/Palladium/Veloce ($M+), Tier 2 Imperas/ARM/Simics ($K-M), Tier 3 gem5/Spike (open), with hybrid_sim positioned at $0
- **9.2 Wins** - cost, Andes-specific output, no FPGA bring-up, customer-shippable path
- **9.3 Losses** - 10,000x cycle-speed gap, M-mode-only today, alpha maturity, single-config hardwiring
- **9.4 Target customer** - mid-tier RISC-V SoC integrators with Andes IP license, priced out of ZeBu
- **9.5 Risks** - Tier-1 price compression, Imperas-under-Synopsys expansion, customer in-house tools, gem5 productization

Because the **vsim leg is Verilator-compiled from Andes RTL** - shipping vsim means shipping Andes IP.

## What hsim's build produces

From `README.md` outputs:

```
build/qemu/qemu-system-riscv64        # QEMU - open source, fine
verilator/build/sim_ax45mpv_premium   # vsim - contains compiled RTL
qemu_plugin/libhybrid_handoff.so      # our plugin - fine
tools/simpoint/bin/simpoint           # UCSD SimPoint - open
```

Only the second one blocks customer shipment.

## Why vsim is the blocker

1. **Verilator translates Verilog/SystemVerilog directly into C++.** The resulting binary embeds the actual microarchitecture - pipeline stages, cache state machines, branch predictor logic, MSHR, ACE. It's not "a model of the RTL", it *is* the RTL compiled to C++.
2. **Cycle-exact behavior is observable.** A determined customer or competitor can probe the binary's responses to crafted inputs and reconstruct cache geometry, replacement policy, predictor tables, etc.
3. **Andes vendor CSRs and undocumented behavior leak.** The RTL knows secrets that are not in public docs (errata workarounds, non-architectural state, debug paths).
4. **Licensing.** Standard Andes IP licenses do not grant the right to redistribute RTL-derived binaries to third parties.
5. **Build dependency.** vsim is built inside a Docker container with the RTL sources mounted. A customer without RTL access cannot even rebuild it.

## Why Alioth IS customer-shippable

- Alioth is a SystemC **abstraction** that correlates with RTL within a small CPI gap. It does not contain the RTL.
- Alioth ships today through Andes' customer channel with the external-vs-internal config split (`WhiteBoxCluster` / `AndesCluster` / `VerificationCluster`) precisely so customers see only what they are allowed to see.
- Alioth's structure (`afw::Module`, customer/internal CCI params) was designed for this exact licensing boundary.

## Net

| Component | Contains Andes IP? | Shippable? |
|---|---|---|
| QEMU + plugin | no | yes (open source) |
| vsim (Verilator + RTL) | **yes - the RTL itself** | **no** |
| Alioth | no (correlated abstraction) | yes (already ships) |
| Wire format / orchestrator | no | yes |

That is why QEMU + Alioth (Section 8) is the only path to a customer-shippable hybrid - the QEMU + vsim version stays internal forever.

## Could hsim ever ship with vsim?

Only with significant carve-outs:
- A "redacted" vsim with cache/predictor parameters stubbed out (loses accuracy - defeats the purpose).
- Cloud-hosted vsim where customers submit jobs but never get the binary (works but heavy ops cost; SaaS model).
- Per-customer NDA + signed RTL license (high-touch enterprise sales; small market).

None of these scale to the mid-tier customer profile in Section 9.4. Hence the recommendation to invest in QEMU + Alioth for the customer-facing path.

message.content: explain ARM's fast mode and cycle mode?

content.text:
ARM ships two simulator product lines for ARM-based SoCs - one fast and functional, one slow and cycle-exact - both customer-shippable, both swappable at runtime.

## Quick comparison

| Aspect | Fast Models | Cycle Models |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Boot OS, develop software | Measure perf, study microarch |
| **Accuracy** | Instruction-accurate (programmer's view) | Cycle-accurate, bit-accurate to RTL |
| **Speed** | 100-500 MIPS | 10-100 KHz simulated clock (~100x slower than Fast) |
| **Timing** | None (no pipeline, no caches modeled) | Full pipeline + cache + memory timing |
| **Built from** | Hand-written C++ behavioral models | RTL compiled via Carbon Model Studio |
| **Shippable?** | Yes (encrypted binaries) | Yes (encrypted binaries) |
| **Typical use** | Pre-silicon SW dev, regression, OS bring-up | Cache sizing, branch predictor tuning, perf eval |

## Fast Models - the QEMU-equivalent in the ARM world

- Functional simulator. Models the **architectural state** (registers, memory, exceptions) but **not the pipeline**.
- Runs ARMv7 / v8 / v9 cores: Cortex-A, Cortex-R, Cortex-M.
- Distributed via ARM Development Studio or as part of ARM IP licenses.
- Uses ARM's **CADI** (Component Architecture Debug Interface) to plug into debuggers, virtual platforms, and other simulators.
- Sold as part of "ARM Fast Models Tools" - architecture-accurate but ~250 MIPS per core typical.
- Customers boot Linux, run UEFI, develop drivers - all without RTL.
- Loose equivalent in the Andes world: nothing exactly. QEMU covers the speed, but Andes-internal QEMU forks (`andescycle-dev-*`) carry vendor extensions.

## Cycle Models - the Verilator-equivalent, but customer-shippable

The trick: ARM owns **Carbon Design Systems** (acquired ~2015). Carbon Model Studio is a tool that takes RTL (Verilog/SystemVerilog) and produces a cycle-accurate, bit-accurate C++ model that is:

1. **~10-100x faster than running the RTL itself in a simulator**, by compiling away wire-level scheduling overhead.
2. **Encrypted** so the customer cannot recover the RTL.
3. **Cycle-exact** - every transaction, every cache miss, every pipeline stall matches RTL.

This solves the exact problem hsim has with vsim: **how do you ship cycle-accurate behavior to a customer without leaking RTL?** ARM's answer: compile RTL into an encrypted C++ binary using Carbon's tooling. Customer gets the binary, runs it, gets cycle figures, cannot extract the RTL.

Cycle Models are sold per-core, per-version. Each ARM core (Cortex-A78, A710, X3, etc.) has a corresponding Cycle Model release.

## The hybrid story - "swap" the canonical pattern

ARM provides Virtual Platforms (via ARM System Generator, Synopsys Virtualizer, or Cadence Virtual System Platform) where Fast Models and Cycle Models share the **same CADI interface**.

Typical customer flow:

```
1. Boot Linux on Fast Model     -> minutes of wall-clock
2. Reach the application's ROI  -> still Fast Model
3. SWAP to Cycle Model          -> trigger at PC / breakpoint / API call
4. Measure the ROI cycle-exact  -> kernel runs at 10-100 KHz
5. Optionally swap back         -> finish in Fast Model
```

The swap moves architectural state (GPRs, system regs, memory) between the two models. The cycle-side cold-starts (caches/predictors empty); customer adds warmup like SimPoint. **Exactly the pattern hybrid_sim implements**, except:

| | ARM Fast + Cycle | hybrid_sim today |
|---|---|---|
| Fast side | Fast Models (ARM-built) | QEMU 9.x (open) |
| Cycle side | Cycle Models (RTL-compiled, encrypted) | vsim (Verilator, NOT encrypted) |
| Customer-shippable | yes | no |
| Speed on cycle side | 10-100 KHz | 5-9 KHz |
| Pattern | RTL -> Carbon compile -> encrypted binary | RTL -> Verilator -> binary (RTL-reconstructible) |

## Why this is the right reference for hybrid_sim / Alioth

ARM proved the **commercial viability** of the customer-shippable hybrid pattern. They charge for both Fast Models and Cycle Models, and big SoC customers buy both. The market gap is real.

For Andes:
- **Alioth ~ Fast Models** in role (customer-shippable, designed for that), but Alioth is *more* than functional - it's cycle-correlated with a small CPI gap. So Alioth straddles the Fast / Cycle line in a way ARM's split does not.
- **vsim ~ Cycle Models** in fidelity, but **not customer-shippable** because Andes lacks the equivalent of Carbon Model Studio's encryption pipeline.

Two strategic implications for the MRD:

1. **QEMU + Alioth** (Section 8 of MRD) gets us most of the ARM Fast + Cycle benefit because Alioth already carries cycle-correlated timing. We do not strictly need a separate "Cycle Model" tier.
2. If Andes ever wants true cycle-exact customer delivery, the path is **encrypted Verilator output**, not unencrypted vsim. That is a Carbon Model Studio-style engineering investment (encryption + protection + license enforcement), not just a "ship the binary" decision.

## What ARM does NOT do that hsim does

- ARM Cycle Models are **per-core**, not per-system. The customer brings their own NoC / memory controller models. Andes Alioth carries the full cluster (MSS, ACE, CM500), which is a richer artifact.
- ARM has no built-in SimPoint clustering or kanata equivalent. The customer integrates separately. Hybrid_sim ships these in-tree.
- ARM does not ship the *trigger / handoff* mechanism as a product feature - it lives in the Virtual Platform tooling layer (Synopsys / Cadence). Hybrid_sim ships the handoff as a first-class binary.

So even at maturity, hybrid_sim's "all-in-one + Andes-specific" packaging is differentiation, not parity.

# Git Commit Messages

The commit message must follow this format (enforced by `.gitea/hooks/validate-commit-msg.py`):

```
type[scope]: description

[optional body]

[optional footer]
```

## Types

- `feat`: New feature
- `fix`: Bug fix
- `refactor`: Code changes that neither fix bugs nor add features
- `test`: Adding or correcting tests
- `chore`: Updates to tasks with no production code change
- `revert`: Reverting previous commits

## Scopes (allowed modules)

- Platform & cluster: `cluster`, `config`, `platform`, `testbench`
- Core: `ifu`, `core`, `lsu`, `mss`, `cm500`, `vpu`
- General: `framework`, `adapter`, `spalib`, `isslib`, `simgen`, `gdb`, `clarity`, `ace`
- Misc: `package`, `demo`, `build`, `docs`, `script`, `skill`, `ci`, `misc`

## Examples (from origin/dev)

**Feature with scope:**
```
feat[d23v-ifu]: add fault handling support & decode flow minor refine
```

**Refactor with detailed body:**
```
refactor[script]: consolidate log utilities and enhance report generation

- Refactored `auto_report.py` to introduce `LogUtil` and its subclasses for better log handling.
- Removed redundant `PatternInfo` class from `regression_info.py` and integrated its functionality into the new structure.
- Updated report generation logic to utilize the new `PatternInfo` class, improving clarity and maintainability.
- Simplified file path handling and command prettification for alioth and tracecompare logs.
- Enhanced error handling in report generation methods.
```

**Bug fix:**
```
fix[ci]: misaligned version caused repo not found error
```

## Subject Style

- Lowercase description after `type[scope]:` (matches repo convention)
- No period at the end
- Imperative mood (e.g., “add”, “fix”, “refactor”, not “added”, “fixes”)
- No hard length limit — be concise but don’t truncate for the sake of 50 chars
- Separate subject from body with a blank line
- Wrap body at 72 characters
- Use the body to explain **what and why**, not how

# Simulator Coding Conventions

Living knowledge base for writing correct, fast Alioth simulator code.
Covers allocation patterns, logging guards, clarity instrumentation, and common pitfalls.
**Update this file** whenever a new pattern or convention is discovered.

---

## Boundaries

### Do NOT modify
- Third-party libraries in `lib/` unless their source code is part of our codebase
  - `lib/Alioth_framework/` — **ours**, can modify
  - `lib/iss_adapter/` — submodule, check before modifying
  - External dependencies installed via Conan — never modify

### Can modify
- Everything under `src/`
- `lib/Alioth_framework/` (our framework code)

---

## Pattern 1: Logging with side effects — use `InplaceLog`

**Problem**: `DebugLog(...)` arguments are always evaluated even when logging is disabled
at runtime. If the call site prepares data (formats strings, builds containers, calls
accessors) just for logging, that cost is paid unconditionally.

**Wrong** — side-effectful work outside the guard:
```cpp
// BAD: rob->RobMonitor() runs even when log is off
std::string info = rob->RobMonitor();
DebugLog("ROB state: {}", info);
```

**Right** — wrap in `InplaceLog`:
```cpp
// GOOD: lambda only runs when kLog is true AND level/filter pass
InplaceLog<afw::debug>([this]() {
    DebugLog("ROB state: {}", rob->RobMonitor());
});
```

**When to use `InplaceLog`**: Any time the DebugLog call requires extra work that would
not otherwise happen — building strings, calling monitor functions, iterating containers,
computing values solely for the log message.

**When `InplaceLog` is NOT needed**: Simple format calls where all arguments are already
computed and cheap (e.g., logging an integer that's already in a local variable).

`InplaceLog<Level>` is a template method on the model base. It checks `kLog` and `kLevel`
at compile time (`if constexpr`), so when logging is compiled out, the lambda body is
eliminated entirely — zero overhead.

---

## Pattern 2: Clarity calls — use `InplaceClarity`

**Problem**: Clarity (pipeline DB dumping) calls do work that's only needed when clarity
recording is active. Without a guard, the work runs every cycle.

**Wrong**:
```cpp
// BAD: BuildClarityRecord() runs every cycle
auto record = BuildClarityRecord();
clarity_db->Insert(record);
```

**Right**:
```cpp
InplaceClarity([this]() {
    auto record = BuildClarityRecord();
    clarity_db->Insert(record);
});
```

All clarity-related calls (DB inserts, record building, counter increments) must be inside
`InplaceClarity`. This is guarded by `kClarity` at compile time.

---

## Pattern 3: Temporary string allocations in hot paths

**Problem**: `fmt::format(...)` or `std::string` concatenation in per-cycle methods
creates temporary heap allocations that show up as hotspots in heaptrack.

**Fixes** (in priority order):
1. Eliminate the string entirely if it's only for logging → wrap in `InplaceLog`
2. Use `std::string_view` or pass format args directly instead of pre-formatting
3. If a buffer is needed, reuse a member variable instead of creating a local each time

---

## Pattern 4: Container reallocation in hot loops

**Problem**: `std::vector::push_back` in per-cycle methods causes repeated reallocation
when the vector isn't reserved.

**Fixes**:
1. `reserve()` with a known upper bound before the loop
2. Reuse a member-level buffer (`.clear()` + reuse vs. allocate new)
3. Use `std::array<T, N>` if the max size is compile-time known and small

---

## Pattern 5: `std::function` overhead

**Problem**: `std::function<void()>` involves heap allocation for non-trivial callables
(closures exceeding small-buffer optimization, typically >24-32 bytes).

**Note**: The `InplaceLog` overload in `base_cpu_top.h` takes `const std::function<void()>&`.
The template version (taking `Func&&`) avoids this overhead. Prefer the template version
for hot paths.

---

## Pattern 6: `sc_time` operations in hot paths

**Problem**: `sc_core::sc_time_stamp().to_double()` and `sc_time` arithmetic can be
surprisingly expensive when called millions of times.

**Fixes**:
1. Cache the time value in a local variable if used multiple times in the same method
2. Avoid unnecessary `to_string()` / `to_double()` conversions

---

# Alioth Architecture

## Module Hierarchy

```
sc_module
  └── LogModule                          # adds spdlog-based logging
        └── afw::Module                  # adds ports, state, config, events
              └── BaseCpuTopComponent     # base for all CPU submodules
                    ├── Core
                    ├── Ifu
                    ├── Lsu
                    ├── Mmu
                    ├── Vpu
                    ├── Ace
                    └── ...
```

## Top-Level Assembly

```
BaseCpuTop
  └── BaseCpuTopTemplate<DynInstT>       # templated on DynamicInst type
        ├── AX46Cpu                      # ax46 core variant
        ├── AX50Cpu                      # ax50 (reuses ax46 pipeline, own MSS)
        ├── AX45Cpu                      # ax45 (own lsu/rob/mshr, reuses ax46 ifu)
        └── D23vCpu                      # d23v (fully separate, own DynamicInst)
```

Submodules are member variables, initialized in the member initializer list of the CPU constructor.

## Core Variants

| Core | Pipeline | MSS | IFU | DynamicInst |
|------|----------|-----|-----|-------------|
| **ax46** | Own (most complete reference) | Shared `MssInterfaceSimple` | Own | Shared base |
| **ax50** | Reuses ax46 pipeline | Own MSS | Reuses ax46 | Shared base |
| **ax45** | Own lsu/rob/mshr | Shared `MssInterfaceSimple` | Reuses ax46 IFU | Shared base |
| **d23v** | Fully separate | Own | Own | Own `DynamicInst` |

Shared across all variants: `BaseCpuTop`, `MssInterfaceSimple`, `Issconfig`.

## Interface Pattern

Interfaces connect modules using `afw::Interface`:

```cpp
// File: <from>_<to>.h
// Class: <From><To>IF
class CoreLsuIF : public afw::Interface {
    // to_initiator() — methods called by the initiator (Core)
    // to_target()    — methods called by the target (LSU)
};
```

Macros: `to_initiator()` and `to_target()` define the direction.

## Cluster Level

```
BaseCluster
  ├── WhiteBoxCluster        -> InternalCluster
  ├── AndesCluster           -> InternalCluster
  └── VerificationCluster    -> InternalCluster
```

`InternalCluster` holds CPU instances via `std::variant<AX46Cpu*, AtomicCpu*, D23vCpu*, ...>`.

Cluster CLI modes and config sources:

| `--cluster-type` | Backend | Config expectation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `whitebox` | `WhiteBoxCluster` | Internal-only. Use `--internal-cfg*`. |
| `andes` | `AndesCluster` | External config through `--external-cfg*`; memory/internal-only settings still come from `--internal-cfg*`. |
| `debug` | Andes-style CLI mode | Same config split as `andes`, plus runtime debug-oriented CLI options such as `--log-level`. |
| `verification` | `VerificationCluster` | Requires both external and internal config and validates them before simulation. |

`debug` is a CLI mode in this tree, not a separate cluster class.

## Key Directories

```
src/model/
├── ax46/                    # AX46 core (reference implementation)
│   ├── ace/                 # ACE coherence
│   ├── core/                # Pipeline stages
│   ├── ifu/                 # Instruction fetch unit
│   ├── interface/           # Module-to-module interfaces
│   ├── memsys/              # Memory subsystem
│   ├── mmu/                 # Memory management unit
│   └── vpu/                 # Vector processing unit
├── ax45/                    # AX45 core
├── ax50/                    # AX50 core
├── d23v/                    # D23V core
├── common/                  # Shared model components
└── top/                     # Top-level model integration

src/config/                  # Configuration definitions per core
src/cluster/                 # Cluster-level models
src/platform_ip/
├── client_visible/          # Platform IPs exposed to customers
└── internal_use/            # Internal platform IPs
src/testbench/               # System-level testbench
lib/                         # Framework libraries (submodules)
```

# C++ Conventions for Alioth

This document covers general C++ conventions. SystemC-specific patterns
(processes, ports, TLM, `afw::State`, CCI config, SystemC pitfalls) live in
[coding-systemc.md](coding-systemc.md). Hot-path logging/allocation patterns
live in [coding-simulator.md](coding-simulator.md).

## Naming

- Functions: `camelCase` (e.g., `getBuildInfo()`, `handleRequest()`)
- Classes/structs: `PascalCase` (e.g., `BuildCollector`, `MshrEntry`)
- Private helpers: `_` prefix (e.g., `_parseLogLine()`)
- Constants/enums: `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` or PascalCase enum values per existing module style

## Language & Tooling

- C++17+ (project uses C++23 via `-DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=23`)
- CMake: follow `doc/cmake-best-practices.md`, target-based patterns, explicit visibility (`PRIVATE`/`PUBLIC`/`INTERFACE`)
- Formatting/lint: `.clang-format` and `.clang-tidy`
- After adding/removing `.cpp` files: run `scripts/generate_cmake_sources.sh`

## SystemC

SystemC process patterns (SC_THREAD/SC_METHOD), constructor conventions, port
naming, TLM, `afw::State`, and CCI config live in
[coding-systemc.md](coding-systemc.md). Read that file before writing any
SystemC module.

## Performance

Performance is a first-class citizen. Avoid "death by a thousand cuts" — a flat profile with no single hotspot is nearly impossible to optimize later.

This section lists high-level principles. For concrete fix recipes
(`InplaceLog`, `InplaceClarity`, container reuse, temporary string elimination)
see [coding-simulator.md](coding-simulator.md).

### Memory & Containers

- **Avoid heap allocations** in hot paths. Reuse long-lived buffers.
- **Prefer `std::vector`** over `std::set`/`std::map` (contiguous > pointer-chasing).
- **Prefer `std::array<T, N>`** when size is truly fixed.
- Keep small values directly in containers, not behind pointers.

### Logic & Loops

- **Lazy evaluation**: don't decode/compute until actually requested.
- **Cache local variables**: copy `this->field` to a local in tight loops.
- Structure loops so the compiler can prove bounds and elide checks.
- Use debug-only assertions for internal invariants.

### SystemC-Specific Performance

See [coding-systemc.md](coding-systemc.md#systemc-performance).

### Logging in Hot Paths

- Ensure logging macros are zero-overhead when disabled.
- Use `InplaceLog` guard to defer argument evaluation in hot paths.
- Avoid complex string formatting inside log calls that may be called frequently.

## Debug Logging

Format: `[Tag] evt=<namespace>.<action> key=value ...`

```cpp
// Good
DebugLog("[LFB] evt=line_fill.commit paddr=0x{:x} set={} way={}", paddr, set, way);
DebugLog("[MSHR] evt=entry.allocate id={} paddr=0x{:x}", id, paddr);

// Bad — free-form prose, no structure
DebugLog("The request for address {} was deferred because the queue is full", addr);
```

### Event Names

`evt=<namespace>.<action>`:
- `req.send` / `req.recv` / `req.accept` / `req.defer`
- `resp.send` / `resp.recv`
- `entry.allocate` / `entry.release`
- `buffer.push` / `buffer.pop`
- `state.change`
- `tlm.read.done` / `tlm.write.done`

### Standard Keys

| Key | Format | Description |
|-----|--------|-------------|
| `paddr` | `0x{:x}` | Physical address |
| `len` | decimal | Transfer length in bytes |
| `uid` | decimal | Request unique ID |
| `trans_id` | `0x{:x}` | TLM transaction pointer |
| `zero_id` | decimal | Zero ID for request tracking |
| `set`/`way` | decimal | Cache set and way |
| `state` | name or decimal | Cache line or FSM state |
| `result` | string | `ok`, `fail`, `defer`, `stall` |
| `reason` | string | Why something happened |

### Value Formats

- Addresses: hex with `0x` prefix — `paddr=0x80001000`
- Sizes/counts: decimal — `len=64`, `qsize=3`
- Booleans: `0` or `1` — `ready=1`, `hit=0`
- Pointers: hex with `0x` — `trans_id=0x7f8a3b4c`

### Traceability

Every request-related log must include at least one correlation key (`paddr`, `uid`, or `trans_id`).

### Log Levels

| Function | Purpose | Availability | Perf risk in info build |
|----------|---------|--------------|-------------------------|
| `DebugLog()` | Detailed flow tracing | Compiled in, runtime-filtered at info+ | **High** — args still evaluate; wrap in `InplaceLog<afw::debug>` if any arg is non-trivial |
| `TraceLog()` | Even more verbose | Compile-time eliminated at `enable_log_level >= 2` | None — body is gone |
| `InfoLog()` | Important state changes | Always emitted | Low (rare callers) |
| `WarnLog()` / `ErrorLog()` | Problems | Always emitted | Low (error paths) |

`--log-level` filters runtime output. Logs removed at compile-time (`enable_log_level`) require a rebuild to recover. When triaging a PR for perf impact, count `DebugLog` adds — `TraceLog` adds are zero-cost in the standard info-level build.

## Doxygen (public headers)

Use `/** ... */` block comments for all public APIs:

```cpp
/**
 * @brief check whether the core should enter the halted mode
 * @details
 * core should call this API in every cycle to check whether the core should
 * enter the halted mode. After entering this mode, the core must wait
 * interrupt event to resume the execution.
 *
 * @param[out] event_inst The instruction that caused the halted event.
 * @return true if the core is halted, false otherwise.
 */
virtual bool OccurHaltedEvent(BaseDynamicInst*& event_inst) = 0;
```

Tags: `@brief`, `@details`, `@param` (with `[in]`/`[out]`), `@return`, `@throw`, `@note`, `@warning`.

# SystemC Conventions for Alioth

This document covers SystemC-specific patterns for Alioth models. For general C++
conventions (naming, language tooling, Doxygen, generic performance) see
[coding-cpp.md](coding-cpp.md). For hot-path patterns and `InplaceLog`/`InplaceClarity`
guards see [coding-simulator.md](coding-simulator.md).

## Process Patterns

### SC_THREAD (dominant — pipeline logic)

```cpp
SC_CURRENT_USER_MODULE = PipelineStage;
// In constructor:
SC_THREAD(mainThread);
// Thread body:
void mainThread() {
    while (true) {
        wait(tick_ & in_valid_.event());
        // ... pipeline logic ...
    }
}
```

- Use for pipeline stages with `while(true) { wait(ev_list); ... }`.
- Synchronize with `sc_event_and_list`: `tick` + `InPort` events.

### SC_METHOD (pin-reactive handlers only)

```cpp
SC_METHOD(onInterrupt);
sensitive << in_irq_;
dont_initialize();  // ALWAYS after every SC_METHOD
```

- Use for interrupts, clock counters, simple combinational logic.
- **Always** call `dont_initialize()` after registration.

### Constructor Pattern

Never use `SC_CTOR`. Use explicit constructors:

```cpp
SC_CURRENT_USER_MODULE = MyModule;

MyModule(afw::Module* parent, const sc_module_name& name,
         sc_event& tick, std::vector<spdlog::sink_ptr>& sink);
```

Use `SC_CURRENT_USER_MODULE = ClassName` instead of `SC_HAS_PROCESS`.

### Event Patterns

- Notifications: `ev_.notify()` (immediate) or `ev_.notify(SC_ZERO_TIME)` (delta).
- No `next_trigger()` — use static sensitivity or `wait()` in threads.
- Avoid cascading `notify()` that cause event storms.

## Port Conventions

| Type | Visibility | Naming | Example |
|------|-----------|--------|---------|
| `InPort` | private | `in_name_` (trailing `_`) | `in_valid_`, `in_data_` |
| `OutPort` | public | `out_name` (no trailing `_`) | `out_ready`, `out_resp` |

- Wire in `Connect()` using `OUTPUT()` / `CONNECT_PORT()` macros.
- Bind SystemC signals in `before_end_of_elaboration()`.

## TLM Conventions

- **AT protocol**: `nb_transport` everywhere for timing-accurate simulation.
- **Debug only**: `b_transport` for debug/backdoor access.
- **Request queuing**: `tlm_utils::peq_with_get` for request/response queuing.
- **Payload lifecycle**: `nds_tlm2_mm` memory manager — always `acquire()` before use,
  `release()` when done.
- **No DMI**: Direct Memory Interface is not used in this project.

## State Management (afw::State)

Use `afw::State<T>` for all clocked state:

```cpp
afw::State<uint32_t> counter_;
// Read current: counter_.cur
// Write next:   counter_.nxt = counter_.cur + 1;
// Commit:       counter_.Tock();
```

Variants: `EnableState`, `RamState`, `MapState`, `FifoState`, `OpState`.

**Critical**: Never modify `.cur` directly — always write to `.nxt`.

## Config Pattern

```cpp
afw::ParamTyped<int> param_queue_depth_;          // internal parameter
afw::CustomerParamTyped<int> param_cache_size_;    // customer-facing parameter
```

CCI broker passed through constructors.

## SystemC Performance

- Prefer `SC_METHOD` over `SC_THREAD` when possible (avoids stack-switching overhead).
- Always call `dont_initialize()` so the process does not run at time zero.
- Use native C++ types (`uint32_t`, `uint64_t`) over SystemC types (`sc_uint`, `sc_int`)
  in hot paths.
- Minimize process activations — avoid wide sensitivity lists.
- Batch multiple logical updates into a single process activation to reduce delta cycles.
- Use `tlm_utils::peq_with_get` for efficient TLM timing management.

For hot-path logging guards, container reuse, and string allocation patterns, see
[coding-simulator.md](coding-simulator.md).

## Common Pitfalls (caught during PR review)

| Mistake | Reason / Fix |
|---|---|
| `SC_THREAD` where `SC_METHOD` suffices | SC_THREAD adds context-switching overhead. If there is no `wait()` mid-logic, use SC_METHOD. |
| Forgetting `dont_initialize()` | Without it, SC_METHOD runs at time zero, possibly before state is valid. |
| Missing `tick` in event-and-list | `wait(in_valid_.event())` without `tick` loses cycle alignment. |
| Event storms | Cascading `notify()` calls trigger chains of process activations in the same delta cycle. |
| Using `SC_CTOR` | Project uses explicit constructors. Never `SC_CTOR`. |
| Using `next_trigger()` | Not used in this project. Use static sensitivity or `wait()` in threads. |
| Wide sensitivity lists | `SC_METHOD` sensitive to many signals when only a few matter. Use specific `sc_event` notifications. |
| Modifying `.cur` instead of `.nxt` | `afw::State<T>` separates current and next. Writing `.cur` bypasses the clock edge and corrupts state. |
| Forgetting `BindEvent()` implementation | New modules must implement `BindEvent()` for the framework event system. |
| Incorrect TLM phase sequence | AT protocol requires `BEGIN_REQ → END_REQ → BEGIN_RESP → END_RESP`. Skipping phases causes protocol errors. |
| Missing `acquire()`/`release()` on TLM payloads | `nds_tlm2_mm`-managed payloads must be reference-counted. |
| Race conditions in `State.nxt` | Two modules writing the same `State.nxt` in the same cycle without arbitration. |
| Unnecessary TLM payload copies | Deep-copying `tlm_generic_payload` instead of passing by pointer with `acquire()`/`release()`. |
| Inconsistent port naming | `InPort` should be `in_name_` (private, trailing `_`). `OutPort` should be `out_name` (public). |

- cc-log: Lightweight system log to record all Claude Code behavior (tool use, subagent creation, compaction, permissions, session lifecycle) for analysis. Use when the user wants to enable/disable behavior logging, analyze Claude Code session logs, list saved logs, or understand Claude Code's tool usage patterns. Trigger on: "cc-log", "behavior log", "system log", "record behavior", "log enable", "log disable", "analyze log".
- code-review: Use when reviewing a PR diff for bugs, logic errors, control-flow mistakes, or correctness issues in C++/SystemC RISC-V simulator code. Used by CI via `opencode run --agent code-reviewer`; also for on-demand reviews.
- alioth-perf-alignment: Systematic counter-driven top-down methodology for aligning Alioth model performance (CPI/throughput) with RTL golden. Walks the full request-response round-trip stage by stage (requester egress → forward path → memory/IP → return path → requester writeback), comparing model counters against RTL FSDB-derived virtual counters at every leg. Use this skill whenever the user debugs a CPI gap or performance mismatch, traces pipeline stalls or backpressure, adds diagnostic counters, compares model timing / throughput / bandwidth / latency with RTL, or asks "why is model slower/faster than RTL" — even if the user does not say "CPI" explicitly. Applicable to any IP path (HVM, PL2C, NC, IFU, LSU, VPU/VSP, ACE, custom IPs). Covers RTL virtual counter design, warmup-vs-steady sequencing, FIFO threshold verification, and the "bottom-up is just top-down on the return path" principle.
- rtl-trace: Use when tracing, analyzing, debugging, or reviewing RTL code (Verilog/SystemVerilog) — timing issues, FSM behavior, pipeline stages, clock domain crossings, signal fan-in/fan-out, or waveform-level behavior. Triggers on Verdi, cycle tables, data hazards, "why does this signal behave this way", "look at this module" or "trace this signal" in a hardware design context.
- fsdb-waveform-analysis: Analyze RTL waveforms from FSDB files using Python ctypes bindings. Use when analyzing signal transitions, checking valid-ready handshakes, comparing FSDB timing with simulation logs, or debugging RTL timing issues. Triggers on requests to view waveform signals, find signal changes, query FSDB data, or compare RTL waveform timing with Alioth model behavior.
- regression-log-structure: Use when debugging a regression failure, reproducing a failing pattern, checking regression pass rate, reading regression results, navigating summary.yaml, or constructing paths to regression output on NAS.
- alioth-timing-analysis: Analyze Alioth model timing and sequencing using the afw framework's tick-tock cycle model. Use when debugging cycle-level behavior, tracing data flow through State/Port/Event chains, understanding thread execution order, or diagnosing timing bugs in SystemC models built on the Alioth framework. Also trigger when the user asks about State cur/nxt visibility, BindEvent ordering, OUTPUT macro propagation mode (tick vs module_event), pipeline latency counting, off-by-one cycle issues, EnableState vs State semantics, CPI gap root cause analysis, backpressure tracing, cross-module Interface data flow, FifoState commit timing, end_of_elaboration event binding, or any question about "when does this value become visible" or "why is this one cycle late" in Alioth model code.
- model-change-review: Use when a model fix or feature is complete and you want a comprehensive static self-check before commit or PR — covers correctness (logic bugs, fault/error risks), design-rule compliance, and simulation-speed hazards. Triggers on "review my model change", "check before PR", "self-review fix", "compliance check", "any bugs in this change", "sim-speed risk on this change". Static only — runtime profiling goes to `sim-profiler` agent.
- regression-info-query: Use when looking up regression patterns or issues for an Alioth core/category, listing tracked regressions, or dumping issue-pattern lists. Backed by `scripts/regression_info.py`.
- agentic-quality-review: Use when reviewing a PR that touches `.agents/` files (agents, skills, rules, droids) for prompt quality, information density, knowledge clearance, and rule adherence. Used by CI via `opencode run --agent agentic-quality-reviewer`; also for on-demand quality reviews.
- gitea-safe-pr: Push the current branch and create or update a pull request on Gitea. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions PR, pull request, submit PR, merge request, push and review, send for review, or wants code pushed and reviewed — even if they don't explicitly say "PR". This skill is REQUIRED for any PR operation in this Gitea-hosted repo. Never use `gh` CLI or raw git push alone for PR workflows. Also trigger when the user says "update PR description", "edit PR title", or wants to modify an existing pull request. Enforces project PR-body rules: include `Related #<issue>` for product-code PRs unless the user explicitly approves a no-issue exception after being asked (skill/CI-only PRs are exempt) and never use Gitea auto-close keywords (close/closes/closed/fix/fixes/fixed/resolve/resolves/resolved) paired with an issue reference.
- cc2oc: Use when setting up OpenCode and need to reuse Alioth agents — converts `.agents/agents/*.md` from Claude Code format to OpenCode agent format.
- module-debug: Use when debugging Alioth simulator behavior with `--log` output — collecting logs, filtering by module instance via `--log-allow-list`, narrowing time windows, navigating `AliothModule.log`. Triggers on "enable simulator log", "why is module X doing Y", "inspect debug log", "filter alioth log".
- sim-speed-profiling: Use when asked to "profile simulation speed", "run perf", "run heaptrack", "find hotspots", "reduce memory", "fix cache misses", "optimize heap allocations", "why is simulation slow", "top-down analysis", "TMA", "flame graph", "IPC", or any host-level CPU/memory profiling question. NOT for cycle-accurate model alignment (use alioth-perf-alignment).
- gitea-api: Manipulate Gitea via the swagger spec at https://gitea.andestech.com/swagger.v1.json; use when asked to automate or call Gitea REST APIs (repos, issues, PRs, releases, users) with correct endpoints, parameters, and auth.
- configure-regression: This skill should be used when the user asks to "update copilot checksum", "update spike version", "update benchmark config", "update regression config", "add a regression variant", "add a regression category", "change copilot_checksum", "bump spike", "update pysimgen version", "modify regression YAML", or needs to add, update, or modify regression config files under .gitea/regression_config/configs/ or version defaults in .gitea/workflows/*.yaml.
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:ralph-loop: Start Ralph Loop in current session
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
